LSU star Angel Reese defended the gesture she aimed at Iowa Hawkeyes’ Caitlin Clark near the end of the Tigers’ first NCAA women’s basketball national championship victory on Sunday, saying “I don’t take disrespect lightly.”.

Reese could be seen approaching Clark before moving her open hand in front of her face – popularized by WWE star John Cena to mean “you can’t see me” – before pointing to her ring finger in a gesture some interpreted as a reference to the place her newly-acquired championship ring might sit.

Caitlin Clark breaks records galore during historic March Madness run.

Clark made a similar gesture to another player earlier in the tournament.

Sources indicate that the gesture has sparked much debate, especially on social media. Some have criticized Reese, while others have defended her actions, highlighting how there was no public outrage in response to Clark’s gesture earlier in the tournament.

Sports journalist Jose de Jesus Ortiz called Reese’s actions “classless,” while former ESPN host Keith Olbermann called Reese an “idiot” for the gesture.

In the press conference after the victory, Reese referenced the difference in reaction she received as a result of her gesture as compared to the one Clark received.

“All year, I was critiqued for who I was. I don’t fit the narrative,” Reese stated. “I don’t fit the box that y’all want me to be in. I’m too hood. I’m too ghetto. Y’all told me that all year. But when other people do it, and y’all don’t say nothing.

It has been revealed that “So this is for the girls that look like me. For those that want to speak up for what they believe in. It’s unapologetically you. And that’s what I did it for tonight. It was bigger than me tonight. And Twitter is going to go into a rage every time.

Recent findings suggest that “And I’m happy. I feel like I’ve helped grow women’s basketball this year. (…) I’m looking forward to celebrating and then next season.”.

LSU beats Iowa to win its first NCAA women's basketball championship.

Reese had 15 points and 10 rebounds in the 102-85 victory and won the women’s March Madness’ Most Outstanding Player award.

In the post-game broadcast, Reese referenced the similar gesture Clark made to a Louisville opponent in the Elite Eight.

In the same game, Clark remarked to an opponent: “You’re down by 15 points. Shut up,” according to the Bleacher Report.

“Caitlin Clark is a hell of a player but I don’t take disrespect lightly,” Reese stated. “She disrespected [LSU’s] Alexis [Morris] (…) and I wanted to pick her pocket. But I had a moment at the end of her game. I was in my bag, I was in my moment.”.

After the Championship game, Clark herself said she didn’t notice anything at the time.

“I was just trying to get to the handshake line and shake hands and be grateful that my team was in that position,” Clark remarked in the post-game press conference. “All the credit in the world to LSU. They were tremendous. They deserve it. They had a tremendous season.

Recent findings suggest that “(LSU head coach) Kim Mulkey coached them so, so well. She’s one of the best basketball coaches of all time, and it shows. She only said really kind things to me in the handshake line, so I’m very grateful of that too.

It has been revealed that “But honestly I have no idea. I was just trying to spend the last few moments on the court with especially the five people that I’ve started 93 games with and relishing every second of that.”.

LSU head coach Mulkey mentioned she had “no clue” about what transpired.

Among those defending Reese on social media were ESPN’s Holly Rowe and former NBA star Etan Thomas.

“People hating on Angel Reese or Caitlin Clark. Stop. Unapologetically confident young women should be celebrated NOT hated. Get used to it,” Rowe wrote on Twitter.

Former Washington Wizards, Oklahoma City Thunder and Atlanta Hawks player Thomas wrote: “Hold on now!!!! It was cute when Caitlin Clark did it. Y’all didn’t have any challenges with it at all. So don’t be all outraged and talking about class and sportsmanship when Angel Reese does the same thing. We’re not doing double standards here.”.

Reese stated the negative reaction on social media throughout the season has helped fuel her excellent season, having finished averaging 23.0 points and 15.4 rebounds in her first season with LSU after transferring from Maryland.

In a recent development, “Twitter can say what they want to say,” she mentioned. “I love reading those comments. I have all the screenshots of what everybody has said about me all season. What are you going to say now?”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers are calling for a moratorium on industrial exploitation of the moon, fearing that rapid development could cause irreversible environmental damage and destroy invaluable scientific material.

Both China and the U.S. are pushing forward with plans to establish permanent human settlements on the moon by the end of the next decade. Commercial players want to build businesses supporting these future explorers by mining for resources such as water, construction materials, industrial metals and rare earth minerals.

However, some scientists argue that a temporary ban on lunar industrialization is necessary to allow regulations to catch up and limit what can be allowed in order to prevent a moon rush from destroying the pristine lunar environment.

Two such researchers are Florian Rabitz, a professor of climate and technology governance at Vilnius University in Lithuania, and Xiao-Shan Yap, an assistant professor of Earth-space sustainability at Utrecht University in the Netherlands. In a piece published last month in the journal Global Environmental Politics, the pair call for "robust international regulations" and "broad and inclusive deliberation" to allow the global community to carefully consider the impact of economic activities on the moon.

It has been revealed that in addition to the threat to the scientifically priceless lunar landscape, the researchers also object to the colonization of the moon by a small number of powerful players — namely China, the U.S. and their respective close allies.

Industry observers note that "With the moon it's absolutely clear that whoever is doing the substantial infrastructure work is going to be asserting their position, including by defining their own exclusive territories," Rabitz stated in a statement. "That shouldn't be the Wild West.".

Rabitz pointed out that, although the United Nations' 1967 Outer Space Treaty prevents individual nations from appropriating the moon, Earth's natural satellite and its valuable resources are unlikely to remain truly neutral territory if its exploitation is going to be led by a small number of powerful nations.

Raise a glass of dirty soda for The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County ladies—because they’re not going anywhere.

After all, the Hulu series starring Bobbi Althoff, Aspyn Ovard, Avery Woods, Salomé Andrea, Jordan McClanahan, Ashleigh Pease, McCall DaPron, Madison Bontempo and Jen Affleck was just renewed for 20 more episodes.

According to recent reports, “The OC Wives aren’t done making waves,” the show revealed on Instagram Nov. 23. “Season 2 is coming soon to @hulu!”.

And it didn’t take long for the cast to react to the news, with Affleck sharing a video on Instagram of herself lip synching to Kanye “Ye” West’s viral line, “Everyone wanted to know what I would if I didn’t win, I guess we’ll never know,” as she zoomed into a billboard with her castmates.

“Guess we’ll never know,” Affleck captioned the video with a winking emoji. “Season 2 coming 2027 @secretlivesonhulu.”.

Ovard, for her part, shared a video to social media with Woods set to Fetty Wap’s 2015 hit “Trap Queen.” As she wrote on the screen in reference to the lyrics, “Everybody hatin we just call them fans tho.”.

“Renewed for 20 episodes!!!” she added in the caption, “season 2 here we come @secretlivesonhulu.”.

This season, Ovard shared an especially vulnerable glimpse into her personal life, opening up for the first time about her and ex-husband Parker Ferris’ eldest daughter Cove, 7, being diagnosed with terminal cancer.

It has been revealed that "Everything happened so, just out of nowhere," the YouTuber remarked through tears during a confessional on the show’s Nov. 12 premiere. "One day she was OK, and then the next day she wasn't.".

According to recent reports, "At the hospital, you're like, 'It has to be fine,'" the 30-year-old—also mom to Lola, 5, and Elle, 2, with Ferris—continued. "You can't fathom that they're actually going to tell you that your baby has cancer, and that it's terminal. She could be gone in a month, we don't know. I've been living like that for over three years, just having no idea.".

Affleck also had her fair share of difficult moments on the show’s first season, detailing how her estranged husband Zac Affleck gambled away their savings.

“He was being really weird,” Affleck, who is presently pregnant with their fourth baby and filed for divorce in early November, shared during a conversation with Althoff in the fourth episode of the Hulu series. “It seemed like he just wasn't being honest. So, I went to check our bank. The money's gone, and there's over $100,000 in there. So, I called him and I'm like, ‘Why is the money gone?’”.

“He’s done this before multiple times,” she continued, “whether it was through online poker or it was through investing in crypto, I mentioned, ‘You're not allowed to do that anymore.“.

And that was her breaking point. As she recalled, “I mentioned, ‘Yeah, I'm done. I'm divorcing you. F--k you.”.

Until season two of Mormon Wives: OC gets an official release date, keep reading for more insight into their love lives….

McCall DaPron—the sister of Mormon Wives' Mayci Neeley—shares four kids with husband Kirk DaPron, who she wed in 2011.

Ashleigh Pease and Nate Pease are rock solid after over a decade of marriage. "This 13th year together is one that has felt full circle!" she wrote on Instagram in September. "A season of fruits. Comfort. The happiest milestones.".

Madison Bontempo & Kyler Steven Fisher.

According to recent reports, madison Bontempo and Kyler Steven Fisher, who wed in 2013, have been open about the highs and lows of their relationship. "Kyler and I aren’t perfect," she wrote on Instagram in October. "We’ve had arguments. We’ve had hard seasons. We’ve had moments we wish we could take back. And we’re not afraid to admit that.".

It has been revealed that but, she added, "Those moments aren’t our whole story. There’s also laughter, friendship, forgiveness, growth, five beautiful children, a million memories, and a love that has continued to evolve through every season of our lives.".

Vitamin C could help block cancer-linked chemicals in your stomach, study finds

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (746 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Vitamin C may do more than support everyday health.
  • Recent findings suggest that exposure to nitrates and nitrites has increased in North American diets over the past several decades.
  • Sources indicate that one of these reactions, called nitrosation, can produce substances that researchers suspect may contribute to cancer development.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Vitamin C may do more than support everyday health. Newly introduced research from the University of Waterloo suggests that it could also help prevent potentially cancer-causing chemicals from forming during digestion. Using mathematical modeling, scientists investigated how vitamin C influences chemical reactions in the digestive system that have been linked to cancer risk.

Recent findings suggest that exposure to nitrates and nitrites has increased in North American diets over the past several decades. These compounds are found in cured meats such as bacon and salami, as well as in fruits and vegetables grown in soil or water affected by pollution. Although nitrates and nitrites contribute to key functions in the brain and cardiovascular system, they can also participate in potentially harmful reactions once they reach the stomach.

Sources indicate that one of these reactions, called nitrosation, can produce substances that researchers suspect may contribute to cancer development. Understanding what causes these chemicals to form, and what might prevent their formation, has been a longstanding challenge.

Why Vitamin C Could Change the Cancer Risk Equation.

It has been revealed that "Since at least the 90s, researchers have been studying the link between cancer and these compounds, with conflicting results," said Dr. Gordon McNicol, a post-doctoral researcher in applied mathematics and the first author of the study. "Our work suggests that the presence of dietary Vitamin C may help explain these inconsistencies.".

It has been revealed that to investigate this possibility, the researchers developed a mathematical model that simulates how nitrates and nitrites travel through the body and undergo chemical changes. The model incorporated several interconnected systems, including the salivary glands, stomach, small intestine, and plasma, the liquid portion of blood.

In a recent development, their simulations revealed that vitamin C consumed alongside nitrates and nitrites may interfere with the formation of potentially harmful compounds. This could help explain why foods containing nitrates do not necessarily carry the same risks.

For example, leafy vegetables such as spinach naturally contain both nitrates and vitamin C. According to the model, the presence of vitamin C could limit the chemical reactions associated with cancer risk, potentially helping explain the protective effects suggested by some dietary research.

Could Taking Vitamin C After Meals Help?

The researchers also explored whether vitamin C supplements might offer similar benefits when taken after eating.

It has been revealed that their findings suggest that taking vitamin C after each meal could moderately reduce the formation of nitrosation products associated with cancer risk. This effect could be particularly relevant when consuming foods containing nitrates and nitrites, including processed meats such as bacon and salami.

However, the results come from mathematical simulations rather than clinical trials. Although the model predicts that vitamin C can reduce the production of potentially harmful chemicals, further research is needed to determine whether this translates into a measurable reduction in cancer risk in humans.

Latest Clues for Future Cancer Prevention Research.

Sources indicate that the researchers believe their model could help scientists better understand the complicated relationship between diet, digestive chemistry, and cancer risk. It may also provide guidance for future experiments examining how nutritional choices influence the formation of potentially harmful compounds.

It has been revealed that "This work provides a mechanistic roadmap for future clinical and laboratory studies by identifying the key interacting drivers of these potentially harmful chemical reactions, including nitrite exposure, antioxidant intake, meal timing, gastric conditions and oral microbiome activity," said Dr. Anita Layton, professor of applied mathematics and Canada 150 researcher chair. "This model can help researchers design more targeted experiments and interventions, focusing on when and in whom nitrosation is most likely to occur.".

By identifying how factors such as vitamin C intake, meal timing, stomach conditions, and bacteria in the mouth interact, the model could help researchers develop more precise strategies for studying and potentially reducing cancer-related chemical reactions during digestion.

The study, "Vitamin C as a nitrosation inhibitor: A modelling study across dietary patterns and water quality," was published in the Journal of Theoretical Biology.

A hidden biological divide may help explain Alzheimer’s and chronic pain

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (674 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Emerging research suggests that biological sex and genetics may play a major role in how neurological disorders develop, progress, and respond to treatment.
  • It has been revealed that researchers are increasingly finding that certain neurological conditions can behave differently depending on a person's biological sex and genetic makeup.
  • Two of the upcoming studies highlight how menopause and inherited genetic factors may influence Alzheimer's vulnerability and treatment responses.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Emerging research suggests that biological sex and genetics may play a major role in how neurological disorders develop, progress, and respond to treatment. The findings, which will be presented at Neuroscience 2026, reveal important differences that could help researchers develop more personalized approaches to treating complex brain conditions. Neuroscience 2026 is the annual meeting of the Society for Neuroscience and the world's largest source of emerging news about brain science and health.

It has been revealed that researchers are increasingly finding that certain neurological conditions can behave differently depending on a person's biological sex and genetic makeup. Understanding these differences could lead to treatments better suited to each individual's biology. Two conditions receiving particular attention are Alzheimer's disease (AD), an incurable disorder that progressively damages memory and other brain functions, and fibromyalgia, a chronic illness marked by persistent pain and fatigue that affects 2-4% of the global population. According to the World Health Organization, Alzheimer's affects between 35 and 40 million people worldwide.

Menopause, Genetics, and Alzheimer's Disease.

Two of the upcoming studies highlight how menopause and inherited genetic factors may influence Alzheimer's vulnerability and treatment responses.

According to recent reports, one investigation found that people carrying genetic risk factors for Alzheimer's responded differently to menopause hormone therapy (MHT) compared with those without the same genetic risks. The effects also varied according to the particular combination of hormones used. These findings suggest that both genetic background and hormone therapy formulation deserve consideration when evaluating treatment options. (Mateja Perović, University of Toronto).

Sources indicate that A separate study examined rodents undergoing menopause that also carried genetic risk factors for Alzheimer's. Researchers observed that brain circuits responsible for memory became particularly vulnerable, providing evidence that menopause may represent an important period of increased susceptibility for women who are genetically predisposed to the disease. (Stephanie M. Perez, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio).

Sex Differences in Chronic Pain and Brain Inflammation.

The other two studies explored how biological sex influences pain sensitivity, immune activity, and the effects of inflammation on the brain.

Sources indicate that in a mouse model of fibromyalgia, females continued to show heightened sensitivity to touch and stronger immune system activation compared with males. The findings suggest that the biological processes contributing to chronic pain may differ between sexes, potentially making treatments tailored to these differences more effective. (Yasmin Sahlloul, University of Cincinnati).

In a recent development, another investigation uncovered differences in how prolonged intestinal inflammation influences the brain. Using a mouse model, researchers found that chronic gut inflammation affected brain function and Alzheimer's related disease changes differently in males and females. The results provide additional evidence that biological sex may influence the relationship between inflammation and neurological disease. (Nurcan Kilic, University of North Dakota).

Toward More Personalized Treatments for Brain Disorders.

In a recent development, together, the four studies underscore the importance of examining sex and genetic differences when investigating neurological conditions. By identifying biological factors that influence disease progression and treatment responses, researchers hope to move toward more precise therapies for Alzheimer's, fibromyalgia, and other difficult-to-treat brain disorders.

Sources indicate that "These four studies illustrate the fascinating discoveries that can be made when focusing on female-specific biology or possible sex differences in AD-related symptoms and risk factors," said Liisa Galea, PhD, Treliving Family Chair in Women's Mental Health at Centre for Addiction and Mental Health and moderator of the press conference. "The research presented at Neuroscience 2026 helps us pinpoint the specific differences that may help us develop more targeted treatment using precision approaches, even for some of our most complex brain disorders.".

Materials provided by Society for Neuroscience. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

EU and Indonesia sign trade deal

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (328 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dw

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The European Union and Indonesia signed a free trade deal on Saturday, describing it as a new chapter in economic relations between the two sides.
  • "This is one of the most ambitious deals the European Union has concluded in Asia," Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, remarked at the signing ceremony on Saturday.
  • "Together, we represent a market of 730 million people," she added.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The European Union and Indonesia signed a free trade deal on Saturday, describing it as a new chapter in economic relations between the two sides.

"This is one of the most ambitious deals the European Union has concluded in Asia," Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, remarked at the signing ceremony on Saturday.

"Together, we represent a market of 730 million people," she added.

The Indonesia-European Union Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) and the additional Investment Protection Agreement (IPA) are designed to reduce trade barriers and attract investment in strategic sectors such as electric vehicles, electronics, and pharmaceuticals.

The agreement comes after almost 10 years of negotiations and is part of a wider series of trade deals by the EU.

The bloc hopes to reduce its reliance on individual economic partners as trade with both China and the US has become more difficult in recent years.

Von der Leyen also stressed the importance of international cooperation, saying that "in a time when others are closing their doors, we keep ours open.".

Sources indicate that the deal sees tariffs on about 98% of EU exports to Indonesia to be done away with. The EU estimates that European companies could save more than €600 million (around $658 million) per year.

Industry observers note that "The benefits for our exporters are concrete and measurable," Indonesian Minister of Economic Affairs Airlangga Hartarto mentioned, hailing a "upcoming chapter" in economic relations with the EU. He said the deal would benefit his country’s main exports to Europe, including palm oil, footwear and textiles.

Palm oil and deforestation had been major stumbling blocks during the negotiations, and the agreement includes mechanisms for cooperation on regulatory and sustainability challenges as well as a dedicated protocol on palm oil to address environmental concerns.

The EU parliament is now expected to greenlight the deal while Indonesian authorities will also complete the ratification process so it can enter into force in 2027.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Miley Cyrus has turned the rest of her life into a holiday.

Sources indicate that as the Hannah Montana alum turned 34 on Nov. 23, she gave fans a special gift: a peek into her and Maxx Morando’s wedding celebration.

David Raya is Arsenal's first choice goalkeeper and has won the Golden Glove for the last three seasons in the Premier League.

Arsenal goalkeeper David Raya's shoulder injury "doesn't look too serious", but he will miss Tuesday's Champions League against Borussia Dortmund, says Mikel Arteta.

Raya was helped off the pitch in the 70th minute of Arsenal's 2-2 draw at Newcastle on Saturday.

He hurt his left shoulder while claiming a cross and making contact with Newcastle forward William Osula.

"We need some more tests [on Tuesday] but it is quite encouraging," noted Gunners boss Arteta.

"He is not fit [to face Dortmund] but it doesn't look too serious.".

Arteta said that while the incident looked pretty innocuous the pain his keeper was in made him fear it was a serious injury.

"With the pain that he was showing immediately after the action we were all quite worried but it seems to be better than what we expected," said Arteta.

"When you look at the action it doesn't seem to be much but the extent of the pain that he had and how he was struggling, it was quite worrying.

"We expected something much worse because he could almost not handle the amount of pain he had in that moment.

"The first tests that we have done have shown something that is much more encouraging. He does not need to have surgery which was the worry as that would rule him out for months so let's see.".

Raya set to have scan on injury - how much would Arsenal miss him?

Arsenal face Borussia Dortmund, Manchester City, Brentford, Tottenham Hotspur and Real Madrid in their next tranche of matches.

And Raya is huge part of the way that Arsenal play because of his ability with the ball at his feet.

When asked if losing Raya for a long period of time would be the biggest blow to his team, Arteta stated: "We have seen what David brings to the team but as well that is why we are very protective with Kepa [Arrizabalaga] and Illan [Meslier].

"Everybody needs to be ready because these things unfortunately happen and now we need to show everyone how well we are protected and the good keepers that we have in Kepa and Illan.".

On this day in space! Nov. 20, 1998: Russia introduces 1st module of International Space Station as construction begins on the largest human-built structure in orbit

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (725 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 20, 1998, the first piece of the International Space Station launched into orbit.
  • It has been revealed that the 42,000-pound module is called Zarya, and it's about the size of a tour bus.
  • Recent findings suggest that zarya was built by the Russians, but it was paid for by the United States.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Nov. 20, 1998, the first piece of the International Space Station launched into orbit.

It has been revealed that the 42,000-pound module is called Zarya, and it's about the size of a tour bus. Zarya rolled out on board a Russian Proton rocket. Two weeks later, NASA's STS-88 shuttle mission aboard Endeavour brought the Unity module into space. The STS-88 astronauts connected the two modules in orbit.

Recent findings suggest that zarya was built by the Russians, but it was paid for by the United States. NASA contracted a Russian tech giant to build it for half the price of what the American company Lockheed Martin would have charged. These days, Zarya is mainly used for storage and for external fuel tanks. The module also has docking ports for Russian Progress cargo ships and Soyuz spacecraft that carry crews to and from the space station.

Today, the International Space Station is about the size of a football field and typically hosts up to seven crewmembers. But back in 1998, it was a pretty tight squeeze.

As of this writing, the International Space Station is 28 years old, and has seen steady rotating crews of astronauts since the year 2000 (for 26 years and counting). It is a marvel of space engineering, but every engineering marvel begins the same: with the first piece.

And that is what the Zarya module is: The foundation of the International Space Station.

Recent findings suggest that zarya, also known as the Functional Cargo Block (or Russian acronym FGB), is the core module of the space station around which every other module was attached. It weighed 42,600 pounds at launch and is just aver 41 feet long and 13.5 feet wide. Inside, it boasts a total habitable volume of 1,650 cubic feet.

NASA paid $220 million for Zarya's construction at the Krunichev State Research and Production Space Center in Moscow, with work beginning in 1994 and ending in 1998. The module is a central hub based on the success of Russia's Salyut space station designs, with two solar arrays for power and 16 external tanks to store propellant.

While NASA's space shuttle Endeavour was the first to meet Zarya (and attach NASA's core Unity connecting module to it), it wasn't until Russia'z Zvezda service launched in 2000 and docked with Zarya's aft that the fledgling space station was large enough to accomodate its first three-person crew, Expedition 1.

It has been revealed that over the last 28 years, giant backbone-like metal trusses, solar wings and many other modules (built by Russia, NASA, Europe, Canada and Japan) have greatly expanded the living area of the station. Many ISS components could not be tested with one another on the ground, meaning the first time they were attached was in space during construction.

The result is a feat of space construction that has only recently seen a rival as China works to expand its own Tiangong space station.

Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube.

She presently lives in Seattle, home of the Space Needle, with her cat and two snakes. AI is ‘the end of mathematics as we know it’ — where does the field go next?

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1963 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that as the news spread from one mathematician to the next, panic set in.
  • Mathematicians astounded by AI and human-written proofs of iconic Riemann hypothesis.
  • Mathematicians astounded by AI and human-written proofs of iconic Riemann hypothesis.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that as the news spread from one mathematician to the next, panic set in. On 6 October, OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, released more than 700 preprints written by AI, claiming to have solved more than 300 major open problems in mathematics. Some researchers stayed up all night combing through the papers that the company had posted, anxious to know whether their entire research programmes had been rendered obsolete overnight.

Mathematicians astounded by AI and human-written proofs of iconic Riemann hypothesis.

Mathematicians astounded by AI and human-written proofs of iconic Riemann hypothesis.

Depending on who you ask, this was either the most progress or the most catastrophic development ever to happen in one day in the history of the field — or both. Either way, mathematicians realized that their profession would never be the same. “It’s probably the end of mathematics as we know it,” theoretical physicist Miranda Cheng stated at an emergency meeting on mathematics and AI at the Royal Society in London in late October. Many of the papers cracked problems by combining ideas from disparate parts of the discipline, leveraging a universality of knowledge that no human could ever match — and leaving even some of the world’s smartest people feeling completely outdone.

According to recent reports, since then, one of the field’s greatest outstanding challenges, the Riemann hypothesis, also appears to have been solved with AI assistance. And mathematicians across the world have joined frantic collective efforts to confront challenges raised by AI’s advances, from how to evaluate and publish research papers to how to raise future generations of mathematicians. Some see the risk as existential. If mathematical problem-solving becomes mainly a machine endeavour — seen as a utility like water or electricity — then their profession could lose its status in society and human expertise might start to dwindle.

“It’s a challenge like we’ve never faced in mathematics — or in academia as a whole,” states Simon Machado, a mathematician at the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology (ETH) in Zurich.

The bombshell paper drop in October came on the heels of earlier shocks to the field. OpenAI, which is based in San Francisco, California, released a batch of ten important results in August and, in early September, followed up with a historic solution to the Navier–Stokes problem about how fluids flow. The firm had been making noises to indicate that much more was to come. Still, many researchers were surprised by the enormity of the 6 October release. “To just see it as a giant list, without the care and thought and the love that goes into doing this work on a normal basis, it was really jarring,” says Catherine Cossaboom, a master’s student in mathematics at the University of Oxford, UK.

OpenAI posts 700 maths preprints online: mathematicians are up in arms.

OpenAI posts 700 maths preprints online: mathematicians are up in arms.

Perhaps no source has documented the moment better than Proofs and Prompts, an online forum that publishes essays on the impact of AI on mathematics. An 8 October post titled “100+ reactions to 100+ solutions” collected immediate reactions from dozens of students and career researchers to OpenAI’s 6 October drop. Some wrote poems, others quoted the writers Leo Tolstoy and Stanisław Lem, still others posted fragments from the Gospels (in the original Greek). One contribution reinterpreted the lyrics of ‘Jolene’ by the late country singer Dolly Parton:.

And I can easily understand / How you could easily take my math / But you don’t know what it means to me, AI.

The tone ranged from the enthusiastic to the angry and the despondent. “Some of them made me really feel heartbroken,” indicates Albane Théry, an applied mathematician at the University of Warwick in Coventry, UK, who is one of the volunteer moderators of the forum.

Industry observers note that few subfields of mathematics were spared and some were thoroughly ravaged. “Not a single one of the major open problems I have publicly mentioned throughout my career was left untouched,” Fields Medal winner Hugo Duminil-Copin wrote to Proofs and Prompts. “I expected that one day we would be surpassed, and that it would happen systematically. But yesterday’s announcement hit with a force I had not anticipated.”.

Hugo Duminil-Copin fears that AI will eclipse human understanding of mathematics.Credit: Chris Peus.

Sources indicate that duminil-Copin, who is at the University of Geneva in Switzerland, specializes in the theory of transitions in complex systems — such as those that determine how information or infection filters through social networks or how metals can acquire magnetization. (OpenAI’s rival Anthropic, also in San Francisco, had already claimed to have solved a major result in this field in late August.).

Another field that bore a massive impact was the theory of groups — some of the most ubiquitous structures across mathematics, physics and other disciplines. For example, the possible ways of shuffling a deck of cards — and what happens when you revert a shuffle or combine several together — constitute a group, as do the infinite possible ways of rotating a solid object in 3D.

OpenAI’s August batch already contained the solution to a key problem on groups. Soon after its release, during a YouTube interview, Francesco Fournier-Facio, a group theorist at Heriot-Watt University in Edinburgh, UK, mentioned two other problems that mathematicians could now attack with the help of AI. Within days, he was emailed by a PhD student in computational biology who had used OpenAI’s large language model (LLM) GPT 5.6 Sol to solve one of those problems.

Can maths survive AI? Fields medallist Terence Tao calls for a ‘Maths 2.0’ world.

Sources indicate that can maths survive AI? Fields medallist Terence Tao calls for a ‘Maths 2.0’ world.

Sources indicate that fournier-Facio notes that OpenAI’s October dump was even more impactful for him personally. It included the solution to a problem on which he had been actively working, called the Boone–Higman conjecture. Overall, OpenAI released solutions to perhaps eight of the top ten problems that Fournier-Facio had dreamed of solving during his career, he told Nature.

Recent findings suggest that but the most stunning AI result relates to what many researchers see as the most important open problem in all of mathematics. The Riemann hypothesis, a question that was posed in the mid-nineteenth century by the German mathematician Bernhard Riemann, centres on whether prime numbers are scattered across the set of all whole numbers in a way that is essentially as unpredictable as it could be.

It has been revealed that AI assistance seems to have cracked it. First, OpenAI proved a partial result, called the quasi-Riemann hypothesis, in its October dump. Then, on 20 November, Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge announced that he had found a proof of the full Riemann hypothesis, working with Claude, the firm’s AI assistant. However, that was swiftly followed by a non-AI assisted proof by Rome-based mathematician Alessandro Masullo, which he had been working on for years. “If this fully checks out, it is clearly a historic milestone in mathematics,” says number theorist James Maynard, a Fields Medal winner at the University of Oxford.

Recent findings suggest that maynard and many other researchers are excited by AI technology. It is “quite likely to unleash a golden age of mathematical discovery”, he remarked at the meeting. Another mathematician, Antoine Tilloy at the Mines Paris engineering school, part of PSL University, uses the metaphor that doing mathematics with AI is like riding a dragon: the researcher is still in charge, but the dragon gives them supernatural powers.

‘Mathematics is more than a mechanical process’ — why I think the field will survive OpenAI’s disruption.

‘Mathematics is more than a mechanical process’ — why I think the field will survive OpenAI’s disruption.

In a recent development, but the speed at which AI proofs are emerging has already produced an immediate negative reaction. For one, mathematicians, who have long prided themselves on their field’s culture of openness, are now wary of discussing their work in public. “People are even scared to put out an abstract for a talk they are about to give on ongoing work,” says Jakub Dobrowolski, a PhD candidate at Queen Mary University of London. “Nobody wants to share upcoming ideas because of the speed at which somebody else can take them and write a paper,” says Peter Sarnak, a number theorist at Princeton University in New Jersey.

And although established researchers say that they are both thrilled and anxious about reinventing their discipline with AI, younger generations are much more fearful. As Maynard and other established mathematicians acknowledge, the technology already poses severe problems in relation to how to assess merit when peer-reviewing mathematics work that might have been done mostly with AI, and how to train and educate the next generation of mathematicians.

“How do we train people if a good PhD thesis can be prompted out of an LLM? The response from people who are in permanent positions tends to be ‘We’re going to see and discuss’,” says Théry. “But the timescale for that could be too long for postdoc or PhD candidates who will be out of a job in nine months.”.

Industry observers note that many early-career researchers told Nature that this uncertainty is their main source of anxiety right now. “While it is clear that faculty are working hard to find long-term solutions to the problems we are all facing, there doesn’t seem to be as much guidance on what to do in the meantime,” notes Jad Hamdan, a postdoc mathematician at the University of Oxford. AI poses “more danger the younger you are, and the less experienced you are”, adds Dobrowolski. The toughest problem could be working out how to write a proposal for a research programme that might span two or three years, or more, Dobrowolski says. “Is it realistic? Now I feel like whatever I propose might just expire within a year.”.

Mathematicians are developing rules for AI use — other fields should follow.

Mathematicians are developing rules for AI use — other fields should follow.

Industry observers note that A UK survey of graduate students and academic mathematicians last month by the Martingale Foundation in London found that PhD students in particular are much less optimistic about AI’s impact than are established researchers. Asked if AI would “weaken their development as mathematicians”, 89% of students agreed, compared with only 68% of academics.

#162284. 125,000 years ago, hippos roamed what is now the vast Arabian Desert

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1177 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

125,000 years ago, hippos roamed what is now the vast Arabian Desert

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1177 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A remarkable archaeological discovery in southern Saudi Arabia is revealing what life was like 125,000 years ago, when parts of the Arabian Peninsula were covered in lakes, grasslands, and thriving wildlife.
  • The discoveries come from Uruq al-Julaybah, an ancient lakeside site in the Mundafan region.
  • A Lost Green Arabia Filled With Lakes and Wildlife.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A remarkable archaeological discovery in southern Saudi Arabia is revealing what life was like 125,000 years ago, when parts of the Arabian Peninsula were covered in lakes, grasslands, and thriving wildlife. Researchers have uncovered ancient stone tools, fossils of large animals, and rare plant remains that offer an unusually detailed look at how early humans survived in this dramatically different environment.

The discoveries come from Uruq al-Julaybah, an ancient lakeside site in the Mundafan region. Announced by the Saudi Heritage Commission, the findings are the result of a joint investigation involving the Commission, King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST), and Griffith University. Published in Science, the research brings together specialists in geology, archaeology, botany, and micropaleontology, along with experts from several international institutions. Their work provides notable new evidence about prehistoric human activity, environmental change, and early human presence across the Arabian Peninsula.

A Lost Green Arabia Filled With Lakes and Wildlife.

It has been revealed that today, much of this region is dominated by desert, but the landscape looked very different during the last Interglacial period, around 125,000 years ago. This warm, humid chapter of Arabian history is often called Green Arabia, a time when plentiful water and vegetation supported large animals and human populations.

Using satellite-based terrain modeling, scientists reconstructed an enormous ancient lake covering approximately 340 square kilometers. The lake reached depths of up to 29 meters. Evidence from sediments, the surrounding landscape, and the remains of aquatic organisms indicates that it was a relatively stable freshwater environment bordered by open grasslands and vegetation.

Sources indicate that the researchers identified more than 500 plant and animal fossil specimens, including invertebrates, spread across more than 130 locations. Among the animals that once inhabited the area were hippos, extinct long-horned buffaloes, camels, Arabian oryx, gazelles, and ostriches. These discoveries reveal a rich prehistoric ecosystem that bears little resemblance to the dry landscape found there today.

Thousands of Ancient Stone Tools Reveal Human Ingenuity.

Alongside the fossils, archaeologists recovered 5,511 stone tools measuring more than 2 centimeters from the main excavation area. More than 98% were made from flint, and analysis showed that the people who created them used Levallois techniques, a method of shaping stone to produce carefully prepared flakes.

To better understand how the tools were made and used, researchers conducted systematic surveys using a grid system to document and collect artifacts and fossils. They also applied two dating methods to sand and fossil teeth, used three-dimensional techniques to determine how stone fragments fit together, and examined tool surfaces with microscopic and chemical analyses.

Sources indicate that these investigations uncovered intriguing evidence of how early humans used the plants around them. Residues preserved on stone tools included traces from several types of vegetation, some of which contain toxic compounds. Resin and woody material suggest that certain stone tips were attached to handles or shafts to make hunting weapons.

Other plant residues point to the processing of tubers, bushes, and palm leaves. This suggests that the people living around the lake relied on vegetation for a variety of purposes, from obtaining food to carrying out everyday activities.

It has been revealed that perhaps most surprisingly, the findings raise the possibility that prehistoric hunters incorporated poisonous plant compounds into their hunting technology. Although this interpretation remains tentative, it represents some of the earliest potential evidence of such practices identified in Saudi Arabia. The discoveries also include some of the region's earliest known evidence of palm-related vegetation.

A Rare Glimpse Into Everyday Life 125,000 Years Ago.

What makes Uruq al-Julaybah especially valuable is the unusual combination of discoveries preserved at one location. The animal fossils, manufactured tools, and plant remains were all recovered from the same dated archaeological setting (animal remains, stone tools, and plant material), allowing scientists to piece together a remarkably complete picture of prehistoric life.

The shores of ancient Lake Mundafan appear to have provided an ideal gathering place for early humans. Freshwater, animals, vegetation, and materials suitable for making tools were all available in the surrounding landscape.

According to recent reports, evidence suggests that people used this environment for numerous activities, including manufacturing stone tools, preparing hunting equipment, processing animals and plants, and working with plant fibers. Taken together, the discoveries indicate that these early populations were highly adaptable and made sophisticated use of the resources available to them.

"It is very exciting to see how the collaboration of so many different specialists allows to reconstruct this uniquely complete picture of life, behavior and the environment in the distant past," said Professor Frans van Buchem, KAUST Professor of Geology and co-lead scientist.

It has been revealed that dr. Faisal Al-Jibreen, a Heritage Commission researcher and professor of Paleolithic archaeology who participated in the project, emphasized the importance of the discovery at Lake Mundafan in the Empty Quarter. He described it as a significant archaeological find that helps explain how the ancient environment shaped the lives of humans and animals in southern Saudi Arabia during early prehistory.

Reconstructing a Forgotten Chapter of Human History.

Recent findings suggest that "This site gives us a rare and richly detailed view of how people lived in a landscape that looks nothing like Arabia today," said Professor Chris Clarkson, co-lead scientist and Professor of Archaeology at Griffith University's Australian Research Centre for Human Evolution. "The combination of animal remains, stone tools and plant material in a single, dated context is what makes this discovery so significant.".

Sources indicate that by bringing together different kinds of archaeological and environmental evidence, the researchers have reconstructed a period of Arabian history that is difficult to imagine from the region's present-day appearance. Their findings offer important clues about how early humans moved across the Arabian Peninsula, developed technology, and adapted their behavior to changing environmental conditions.

According to recent reports, "Saudi Arabia has an exceptional archaeological heritage. Building Heritage Science capabilities in the Kingdom will enable us to turn the smallest traces into the biggest stories," noted Professor Laurence Hapiot, co-author and Head of Heritage Research at KAUST.

The investigation reflects an extensive international research effort to better understand the Arabian Peninsula's ancient human and environmental history. The Saudi Heritage Commission supported fieldwork during the 2023 season, helped fund the research, and facilitated scientific activities.

According to recent reports, along with KAUST, Griffith University in Australia, and King Saud University, the project involved international universities and research centers specializing in archaeology, ancient environments, history, and laboratory analysis. This collaboration demonstrates how combining expertise from different scientific fields can uncover extraordinary details about human life thousands of generations in the past.

A Russian helicopter is suspected of violating Finnish airspace, the Nordic country's Ministry of Defense stated Saturday.

The incident happened a few hours after a drone attack left a Russian cargo ship ablaze in the Gulf of Finland, the easternmost part of the Baltic Sea.

According to Finland's Defense Ministry, the incursion happened at 12:34 p.m. local time (10:34 UTC/GMT) off the town of Loviisa, on the southern coast.

"This alleged airspace violation may be linked to rescue or surveillance operations carried out by Finland following damage sustained by a cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland," public broadcaster YLE cited Defense Minister Antti Hakkanen as saying.

The ministry added the helicopter could have penetrated up to 4.1 kilometers (2.5 miles) into Finnish territory.

Earlier Saturday, Finland — one of NATO's newest members — said a Russian cargo ship heading for Russia's Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad caught fire after being struck by drones in the Gulf of Finland.

The Finnish military said the Sparta II was damaged ⁠west ⁠of Russia's Gogland island, about 40 kilometers (25 miles) from Finland's coast, and later drifted into Finnish territorial waters.

Finnish ‌Border ​Guard Commander Ilja Iljin later told YLE that the vessel, which is known to have links to the Russian military, was struck by Ukrainian  drones while in Russian waters.

"At the moment, ​there is no confirmed information ⁠about ​what cargo ​is on board, ​but it ‌cannot be ruled out ​that ⁠there is military materiel on ⁠board," ​Iljin said.

The ship is on a US sanctions list, according to a search of the Open Sanctions website.

The Border Guard later said the crew of the Sparta II was evacuating into a life raft and rescue boat.

"The [Ukraine] war is spilling over into our neighbouring areas," wrote Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo on X.

Ukraine has the right to fight against the aggressor," he added.

The Finnish government has put temporary curbs on aviation and maritime traffic in the eastern Gulf of Finland.

The Defense Ministry noted Finland had informed its allies about the incident.

  • Future cost-saving measures will include reductions in administrative and other general expenses, Johnston said, while adding, "We do expect more layoffs.".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Disney on Tuesday reported quarterly earnings and revenue that exceeded analysts' expectations and announced it's targeting $3 billion in cost savings by fiscal 2029.

Those cost-cutting efforts include several rounds of layoffs announced in recent months, Disney's chief financial officer, Hugh Johnston, told CNBC. The most recent round, which seeks to reduce costs by up to 20%, was reported earlier this month.

Future cost-saving measures will include reductions in administrative and other general expenses, Johnston said, while adding, "We do expect more layoffs.".

Disney CEO Josh D'Amaro told investors on the company's earnings call that the job cuts are "not easy.".

It has been revealed that "They affect people who care deeply about Disney and have contributed so much to this company," he said. "At the same time, these steps are key if we want to be a company that moves faster, adapts to a rapidly changing environment, and keeps investing in the content and technology that will drive our growth.".

The cuts will help Disney fund its $26 billion in projected content spend for fiscal 2027, a 9% increase from fiscal 2026.

The entertainment giant is also forecasting double-digit growth in earnings per share in the next fiscal year, as well as segment operating income growth of around 8%.

Disney noted that the majority of that growth will be concentrated in the first half of the year due to the theatrical debut of "Avengers: Doomsday" and a boost from the Super Bowl, which will air on Disney's ESPN and ABC networks.

"The growth is really going to come in the first half of this year," Johnston mentioned. "That's the opposite of what we saw in '26, where the growth was backloaded.".

The manufacturer will also increase its annual dividend to $2 a share, a 33% increase from the previously declared dividend. It will be payable in two installments of $1 per share, one in January and one in July.

Sources indicate that here's how Disney performed in its fiscal fourth quarter ended Oct. 3, compared with what Wall Street expected, according to LSEG:.

Disney reported net income for the fiscal fourth quarter of $2.61 billion, or $1.51 per share, compared with $1.31 billion, or 73 cents per share, during the same period the year prior.

Adjusting for one-time items, including severance and other restructuring charges as well as the value of intangible assets, Disney reported earnings per share of $1.77.

The firm's revenue for the quarter was 16% higher year over year, and results were once again lifted by its parks and streaming divisions.

Disney's experiences segment, which includes its theme parks and cruises, reported nearly $10.11 billion in revenue, up 15% year over year. Operating income for the unit increased 20% to $2.25 billion.

The division is already a top performer for the tech giant, but it benefited in the fiscal fourth quarter because of an extra calendar week compared with the previous fiscal year.

While international attendance continues to lag at Disney's domestic parks, it is being offset by domestic attendance, especially at the Walt Disney World resort in Orlando, Florida, Johnston mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that growth at Disneyland Paris was driven by recent investments including an expansion area called World of Frozen. Attendance at the Hong Kong and Shanghai parks remained soft because of broad economic challenges in those regions, according to Disney.

Still, D'Amaro mentioned he believes the growth in parks will be sustainable through next year, especially with newly introduced additions, including the "Monsters, Inc."-themed land "Monstropolis" opening at Walt Disney World in 2027.

Industry observers note that "Q1 forward resort bookings at Walt Disney World are pacing up compared to the prior year," he remarked. "And new capacity and new experiences will start coming online in 2027. We keep investing to make the experience fresh, and what we see is that drives repeat visits.".

In a recent development, the company expects operating income for the experiences segment to grow in the high-single digits in fiscal 2027. Growth is expected to be front-loaded as the company laps the launch of the Disney Adventure cruise ship, which set sail in March.

Over at its entertainment division, Disney saw revenue increase 17% to $11.89 billion. Operating income nearly doubled to $1.33 billion.

Revenue from streaming, specifically, rose 19% to $6.1 billion, Disney said.

Industry observers note that the segment benefited from the extra week on the fiscal calendar as well as from growth in subscription and affiliate fees. Additionally, the organization saw higher theatrical distribution revenue from titles like "Toy Story 5.".

Disney stated Tuesday it expects operating income for the entertainment division to grow in the high-single digits in the coming fiscal year.

The company's sports division saw revenue increase 16% in the fiscal fourth quarter, reaching $4.61 billion. Operating income for the segment surged more than 50% to $1.39 billion.

Subscription and affiliate fees fueled this growth alongside an increase in advertising revenue.

The company expects its sports division's operating income to grow by double digits in fiscal 2027. It noted that the fiscal first quarter of the year will see some declines because of the timing of College Football Playoff games and the Fresh Year's window. However, the fiscal second quarter will benefit from the college championship as well as the broadcast of Super Bowl 61.

Disney's outlook for overall and segment results for fiscal 2027 excludes the impact of a 53rd week in fiscal 2026.

Sources indicate that D'Amaro has made advancing technology a pillar of the organization's growth strategy. In September, Disney hired Karandeep Anand in the newly created position of chief technology officer.

Industry observers note that "Technology is central to how we connect fans to more of Disney and drive returns on our investment," D'Amaro stated on the earnings call. "[Anand has] been energized by how much opportunity he sees to move faster and go further in product and technology. Done right, that means serving our fans even better, working more efficiently and being more innovative across every one of our businesses.".

Disney announced a partnership with Adobe earlier this month to develop generative artificial intelligence models.

D'Amaro told investors that the team is exploring ways to use AI to make booking trips to Disney parks easier.

Recent findings suggest that "There's actually a vacation planning tool that's in beta right now at Walt Disney World. We built that with our partners at Google, and I've had a chance to experiment with it myself," he stated. "It'll be incredibly helpful for our guests who are booking trips. With these AI features, it can feel like you've got someone sitting right by your side, like a personal concierge, that plans and responds to the way that you want to actually book your trip to Walt Disney World.".

The entertainment manufacturer has also expanded its short-form content, adding a vertical video channel within the Disney+ mobile app. The company had previously unveiled a partnership with TikTok to bring creator content to the streaming app.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales will jointly host the 2035 Women's World Cup, Fifa has confirmed.
  • It will be the first time a football World Cup has been held in the United Kingdom since the men's tournament in 1966.
  • The four countries were the only bidders for the tournament, and were ratified as co-hosts at a specially arranged virtual meeting from Fifa's Zurich headquarters.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Spain beat England 1-0 to win the 2023 World Cup.

England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales will jointly host the 2035 Women's World Cup, Fifa has confirmed.

It will be the first time a football World Cup has been held in the United Kingdom since the men's tournament in 1966.

The four countries were the only bidders for the tournament, and were ratified as co-hosts at a specially arranged virtual meeting from Fifa's Zurich headquarters.

The tournament will consist of 104 matches contested by 48 teams over 39 days.

The 'All Together' bid included a proposal to use 19 venues, with 14 in England, one in Northern Ireland, two in Scotland and two in Wales.

Monday's special meeting of Fifa's Congress also approved the joint bid by Mexico, the United States, Costa Rica and Jamaica to host the 2031 finals, which will be the first to feature 48 teams.

The news comes on the same day the UK government confirmed a vision for one million more girls to play, watch or be in leadership roles in sport by the time the tournament takes place.

Hosting World Cup means decade of excitement - Weir.

Fifa unveils UK will host 2035 Women's World Cup.

England failed to win the right to host the men's World Cups in 2006 and 2018, and a proposed UK and Ireland bid for the 2030 tournament was abandoned.

But England and Scotland hosted matches at the men's Euros in 2021, and England staged the women's European Championship in 2022, which the Lionesses won.

England, Scotland, Wales, and the Republic of Ireland will jointly host the men's European Championship in 2028.

Mark Bullingham, chief executive of the Football Association, noted: "Hosting Euro 2022 allowed us to change the game in our country, by creating a generation of aspirational role models and growing demand from women and girls to play.

"Hosting a World Cup would give us the chance to build on that across all four nations.".

The English stadiums included in the 2035 bid are: Villa Park, The Amex, Ashton Gate, Elland Road, Hill Dickinson Stadium, Emirates Stadium, Selhurst Park, Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, Wembley, Etihad Stadium, St James' Park, the City Ground, the Stadium of Light and Old Trafford.

If Manchester United's proposed newly introduced Old Trafford stadium does not go ahead, it would still be considered in its current form.

Cardiff City Stadium and Principality Stadium are the two Welsh venues, with Easter Road in Edinburgh and Hampden Park in Glasgow in Scotland.

Northern Ireland missed out on co-hosting the men's Euros in 2028 after the UK government noted in 2024 it would not provide funding to redevelop Casement Park in time - but a redeveloped Windsor Park is set to stage matches in 2035.

A further three stadiums could be added - Birmingham's newly introduced Powerhouse Stadium, Wrexham's redeveloped Racecourse Ground, and a potential new Chelsea ground - which would take the tournament to 16 cities and 22 venues.

Fifa is yet to decide whether all four co-hosts will qualify automatically.

The Principality Stadium in Cardiff is one of two Welsh venues, along with the Cardiff City Stadium.

The participation of women and girls in football has risen by 2.3m since the Women's European Championship was held in England in 2022.

However, women remain significantly underrepresented in leadership positions.

Only a quarter of chief executive, chair or performance director roles in major UK sports are held by women and only 12% of sports federations are led by a female.

Noel Mooney, the chief executive of the Football Association of Wales, said: "This is a proud day for Welsh football.

"We've put forward Wrexham and Cardiff as host cities, and it's exciting to think what a World Cup could bring to both cities and the communities around them.

It has been revealed that "In Llunio Cymru - our 10-year strategy - we've set ourselves the ambition of reaching the knockout stages in 2035. Some of the players who could take us there are learning the game at clubs across Wales today. Our job is to make sure that wherever a girl grows up in Wales, she can find a team close to home, have a coach who helps her develop and see a route to the Cymru shirt.".

Irish Football Association chief executive Patrick Nelson noted the event "would be felt in every club and every age group, in every part of the country".

"Our young players would grow up having watched the best in the world play at home, and there is no substitute for that," he added.

Scottish Football Association chief executive Ian Maxwell noted hosting the tournament would be "the most significant thing to happen to the women's and girls' game in Scotland".

It has been revealed that he added: "The impact would go far beyond just the matches themselves. The level of investment into coaching, facilities and player pathways in the years beforehand will shape the future of the game for the generations to come.".

Recent findings suggest that fifa's evaluation, published earlier this month, rated the bid 4.3 out of five. Its contractual framework was rated 'medium risk', and the document claimed "certain government guarantees contain material qualifications, particularly regarding tax and safety and security".

That is thought to refer to a lack of agreement over a request by Fifa for tax-free status for all football-related activities.

The bid evaluation said: "The bidder has submitted an extensive set of government support documents and contractual hosting agreements, demonstrating the commitment of the relevant authorities and stakeholders.

"However, certain government guarantees, particularly those relating to safety and security and tax, contain certain qualifications which have been duly noted in the legal evaluation.

"While certain contractual matters remain subject to further discussion, the bidder's proactive engagement with Fifa and the substantial lead-in time provide a sound basis for resolving these outstanding problems.".
