#162279. Goodbye, World: The End of Programmers

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2451 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Goodbye, World: The End of Programmers

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2451 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that becoming a programmer was, for me, a compromise.
  • The switch came with a sense of shame, which in retrospect had a whiff of melodrama.
  • Recent findings suggest that but I don’t think my squeamishness was entirely misplaced.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that becoming a programmer was, for me, a compromise. Midway through my junior year of college, it became clear that, as an international student from Korea, I likely wouldn’t be able to stay long after graduation unless I changed my major from philosophy to a STEM field that made me eligible for a visa extension. The obvious choice was computer science, which was already my minor.

The switch came with a sense of shame, which in retrospect had a whiff of melodrama. I suppose I was afflicted by what Ian McEwan once called “modern forms of snobbery” in describing a character who, after her bookish college education, came to consider “a man with a degree in chemistry incomplete as a human being.” Chemistry, computer science—same diff. It’s safe to say I did not have many friends in the CS department.

Recent findings suggest that but I don’t think my squeamishness was entirely misplaced. In the post-Facebook-IPO ferment of the 2010s, this country’s computer science departments were newly flush with a certain breed of striver who in another era would’ve gone to Wall Street. My theory is that many in America who acquired a hostility toward technology acquired it by way of a hostility toward these upstarts. That is to say, they aren’t so much anti-technology as anti-technologist.

According to recent reports, in any event, I half-assed my way through a good many CS assignments, which meant I was never in danger of going to grad school for AI. But by virtue of a robust public math education in Korea, my entry into the subject was, mercifully, not too bumpy. If anything, theoretical computer science and distributed systems seemed like a continuation of philosophy.

But I could not dispel the sense that programming was a frivolous waste of energy. Every line of code I had to read, every line of code I had to write, was a theft of the time I could’ve spent reading something I cared about. Perhaps it didn’t help that my first two languages were Java (hideous and tedious) and C (admirable but unforgiving). To this day, Java code is like a poisoned madeleine that brings back unwelcome memories.

It has been revealed that after college, my visa dictated that I take a job directly tied to my major, and I found a tech organization willing to sponsor my green card. The concern was, it could be any number of years until I got the green card—four, it’d turn out—so I figured I might as well find a way to make programming pleasurable.

The first couple of months on the job were joyless. I worked at a health care startup, which I thought gave me a serviceable sense of moral cover against the ongoing techlash and a way to indemnify myself later as a writer. But I liked my coworkers, some of whom also harbored artistic ambitions, and after work we’d regularly adjourn to literary events at the McNally Jackson, a block from our office.

Recent findings suggest that then, one day, I discovered a language called Haskell. I was tasked with rewriting a code base using a library that borrowed concepts from it. My vague impression of Haskell had been that it was a difficult language involving a branch of mathematics called category theory. There was something seductive about the intimidating aura around it, and when I tried my hand at writing basic programs, the language was indeed challenging, but appealingly so.

I started lurking in Haskell forums where researchers in the field of programming languages—“PL,” as it’s known—flaunted their lavish command of the language. PL researchers might as well be the poets of computer science: a small community of attentive monomaniacs who engaged in a largely unprofitable enterprise—a rarity in computer science—with all the attendant beef and infighting. The unprofitability meant that, unlike AI, the field had an incorruptible dignity to it.

Soon, to my surprise, I found myself programming outside work. After months of tinkering with Haskell, I discovered a book titled Writing a Compiler in Go. Turns out you could even invent a language yourself. I made a few toy languages, useless in practice but invaluable for demystifying how programming languages work.

According to recent reports, there was also an oblique way coding could help writing. In Draft No. 4, John McPhee, the journalist’s journalist, says that he still uses an ancient text editor called Kedit, recommended to him in 1984 by a programmer at Princeton. (“I have never used a word processor,” he writes.) When I switched to a text editor myself, I could see why he’d stuck with it. With open source code, I could add silly but useful features, such as highlighting “TK”—a common shorthand in journalism for placeholder text—in a conspicuous color so that it was easy to locate later.

If nothing else, I came to appreciate that programming was a reliable way to enter that elusive mode called flow, a state in which we’re somehow forgetful and alert at once.

It has been revealed that in the industry, there’s a general impression that fussing over programming languages is juvenile. If a job candidate expresses enthusiasm for languages, it could very well be a red flag. Being a “polyglot” is no virtue if you can read a menu in five languages but can’t write decent prose in one. And per the popular and influential essay “Choose Boring Technology,” using fancy, novel languages is at odds with serious, robust engineering—akin to how avant-garde poetics are unfit for drafting legal contracts.

Industry observers note that unfortunately for my employers, I had precisely zero fucks to give about serious engineering. I did, however, give a great many fucks about having a pleasurable time at my day job until I received the green card. I took on projects if they’d give me an opportunity to use a new language, which is a dumb reason, and for the same reason even volunteered to change teams, usually a bad career decision. At the obligatory company hackathon weeks, I hacked together domain-specific languages—those specialized for a narrow purpose. I made a meager public contribution by submitting a couple of low-hanging patches to the official TypeScript compiler. I picked up a few gold badges on Stack Overflow. The years went by and, what do you know, I became a pretty decent programmer.

Then everything changed, as it did for everyone else, in November 2022. When ChatGPT arrived, it was a wild card whose impact on the industry was far from obvious. Using neural networks to write code wasn’t latest. Early readers of Andrej Karpathy’s blog will remember the 2015 post featuring plausible-looking C code generated by an LSTM—a precursor of the transformer—which nonetheless amounted to little more than a parlor trick.

Sources indicate that I remember tasking GPT-4 with rewriting a simple JavaScript program in different languages. It performed like Google Translate, instantly and passably. I likened ChatGPT to the monkey’s paw from the eponymous horror story, the accursed object that grants your wishes but not without casualties. In dutiful pursuit of the given objective—and only that objective—LLMs produced a locally correct solution while mangling essential code around it.

Recent findings suggest that then, in early 2025, AI command-line tools were released. At first, what I saw wasn’t so much a leap in quality as a greater eagerness to volunteer help. Then they improved—at this point I should quote Hemingway’s line about how one goes bankrupt—gradually, then suddenly. Within a year, they became massively, belittlingly better at my job.

Some engineers still labor a great deal to remain unimpressed, quibbling about how “it’s good at X but not yet at Y.” Please. The flaws are there, sure, and guardrails are essential. But a better heuristic for their usefulness would be: If you had to choose, for the rest of your life, between pair-programming with a competent colleague and these tools, which would you want? Any programmer worth their salt must acknowledge that they won’t be as useful to their colleague as these tools are. Even if the colleague were Linus Torvalds, I would choose the LLMs, since they won’t give me hell for asking dumb questions.

In a recent development, for someone who feels no allegiance to tech, the usefulness of these coding tools triggers contradictory emotions. I find ChatGPT’s indecorous entry into the literary world intolerable, and I remember feeling a creeping nihilism about the writing profession when it was released. I know firsthand what a reliance on AI can do. As I’ve come to rely more on coding tools to hand me solutions, my ability to code has gone through a swift and decisive decline. Depend on it to write sentences and it will, like a neurodegenerative disease, blunt the finer senses that writers must protect the way pianists protect their hands.

Industry observers note that earlier this year, it was reported that more than 90 percent of code at companies like Anthropic and Coinbase is written with AI. As most people are prompting rather than hand-coding, much of modern software engineering has become machine-operated, not unlike Mitch McConnell these days.

Industry observers note that while this may not be the end of programming, it’ll be the end of programmers. To keep calling those in this profession “programmers” would be incorrect, since the entity that does the programming is a platoon of agents, with humans at desks prompting something out of them. A more flattering term might be meta-programming, but it’d be more accurate to say that programmers have become operators of sorts.

Recent findings suggest that an operator is someone a degree removed from the thing they manipulate. (Unlike someone chipping at rock with a pickaxe, an operator of mining equipment never touches it.) Perhaps one way to describe how the nature of the profession has changed is that it’s as if cooks had stopped making food themselves and taken to writing recipes instead. If you’ve spent any time around AI Twitter, you might be forgiven for thinking that software engineering is now about looking impressed by markdown files.

Recent findings suggest that this isn’t necessarily something to be defeatist about, and I’m not pessimistic about the quality of engineering. When coding agents were first released, I wasn’t sure whether this was just another natural progression, since the story of programming is a story of ever higher levels of abstraction. From bytes to assembly to higher-level languages like Python, we’ve built tools to domesticate the complexity. And with AI, we’ve finally handed off tasks that are constitutionally unfit for the human brain.

But as programmers cede control over the final unit of manipulation, programming no longer qualifies as a craft. Hence my disagreement with Simon Willison, otherwise a voice of reason among witless clout chasers in AI discourse, who wrote, “Quitting programming as a career right now because of LLMs would be like quitting carpentry as a career thanks to the invention of the table saw.” With all due respect, this is a flawed analogy, as carpenters working with a table saw are still craftspeople.

According to recent reports, this means there won’t be great individual programmers in the way that someone like Brian W. Kernighan was: the programmer laureate who cowrote what is possibly the greatest book on programming, The C Programming Language, by which we measure programming languages to this day. (It is the book that popularized the “Hello, World” convention.).

Sources indicate that another loss is that programming no longer induces the flow state—or it induces a shallow sort of flow at best. There’s still a certain “hookedness” to the activity, but whereas tackling a gnarly bug once meant begging every individual neuron in my brain to do its part, the work has become suspiciously effortless. That hookedness may be closer to what the cultural anthropologist Natasha Dow Schüll called, in her 2012 book Addiction by Design, the “machine zone,” the trancelike state of the Las Vegas gambler.

Even though I’ve stopped coding myself, I find I’ve been producing more code than ever before. The features I’d built for my open source editor in the past were unserious enough that I could bang out a quick program on a weekend afternoon or two. But with Claude Code, I’ve become addicted to making what has essentially become a heavyweight word processor, a juiced-up Scrivener. (My changelog tells me I’ve built 239 features and 17 extensions, mapped to 141 keyboard shortcuts.).

One Sunday this summer, I was disconcerted to discover that I’d spent 10 hours in Claude Code. How do I know? I used Claude Code to build a time-tracker for Claude Code usage. I resolved to cut back. I spent eight hours the next day. This compelled me to write a program, using Claude Code, to block myself from Claude Code except for two days a week, which I of course tried to undo with Claude Code, only to be valiantly defended by Claude Code.

Sources indicate that with this borrowed competence has come a total loss of interest in learning latest languages. A couple of years ago, an iOS meditation timer app I’d used for years started nudging me with ads, and I resolved to one day learn Swift, the language Apple created for iPhone and Mac apps, and build a simple version myself. But I now know that’s never going to happen, because I’ve already built it knowing zilch about Swift syntax, along with 12 more iOS and Mac apps: The machine helped me fork the long-unmaintained SelfControl into a more granular internet blocker; by reverse-engineering a clipboard manager—I was never sure it wasn’t leaking my input—it built a new one with an auditable security profile.

Sources indicate that I suspect, going forward, that I’ll still mess around with code, but no longer as a professional. Recently, it became clear that I needed to quit my day job as a programmer to finish a book I’d set out to write. I once told a writer friend that I’d try to be a mole in this industry as long as I was in it. I did get to see some things while I stuck it out and, along the way, coaxed that green card from my employer.

I’m not too sorry to leave this profession at this moment of nuttiness. But I’ll admit that, after all those languages I enlisted to make my detour more tolerable, I came to appreciate the pleasures of polyglot programming. As humans cede control to the machine, it’ll be a joy lost to us all.

This is the final installment in a three-part Machine Readable series on AI-enabling languages. It may also be the final Machine Readable column, period.

Chelsea searches for upcoming manager as Premier League breaks record for most sackings in a single season

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It was just six months ago that Graham Potter was deemed the man to usher in a fresh, exciting era at Chelsea.
  • The club’s fresh ownership group, led by American businessman Todd Boehly, had enticed Potter away from Brighton with the promise of managing one of the most lucrative teams in world soccer.
  • More than $600 million was spent on bringing big-name players to the club and Potter, one of the most exciting young managers in the Premier League, was to mold them into a winning machine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It was just six months ago that Graham Potter was deemed the man to usher in a fresh, exciting era at Chelsea.

The club’s fresh ownership group, led by American businessman Todd Boehly, had enticed Potter away from Brighton with the promise of managing one of the most lucrative teams in world soccer.

More than $600 million was spent on bringing big-name players to the club and Potter, one of the most exciting young managers in the Premier League, was to mold them into a winning machine.

It has been revealed that chelsea has spent over $600 million on fresh signings. Here's why that's significant.

But, on Sunday, the club announced that it had sacked its manager after an underwhelming spell in charge.

Potter managed to win just 10 of the 28 league matches this season and leaves the team 11th in the Premier League table.

In recent weeks, players had looked a shadow of their former selves and many fans had lost confidence that Potter’s initiative for the club could ever work.

Eventually, after previously sticking by its manager, Blues ownership agreed.

“On behalf of everyone at the club, we want to thank Graham sincerely for his contribution to Chelsea,” the club’s co-owners Todd Boehly and Behdad Eghbali said in a statement.

“We have the highest degree of respect for Graham as a coach and as a person. He has always conducted himself with professionalism and integrity and we are all disappointed in this outcome.”.

In his previous role as Brighton manager, Potter was given time to stamp his identity on the squad.

The club was punching above its weight financially and, as a result, carefully selected latest signings which would compliment Potter’s style of play.

The approach paid off as the team became an established Premier League outfit which has gone on to greater things this season – the Seagulls at the moment sit sixth in the league and in the UEFA Conference League qualification spot.

At Chelsea, it seemed the complete opposite.

As was the case under previous owner Roman Abramovich, the club expected instant results and used its financial weight to sign a number of high-profile names, including the likes of Enzo Fernández and Mykhailo Mudryk.

Despite his impressive CV, Potter had never managed superstars and suddenly found himself in a changing room with multiple.

The scatter gun approach to recruitment also left the team lacking balance and organization with Potter failing to get a tune out of a team busting with talent.

In truth, many had raised an eyebrow when Potter, inexperienced at the very top level, was chosen to replace Thomas Tuchel as manager.

Despite falling out of favor with fans by the end of his tenure, Tuchel had guided Chelsea to the Champions League title in 2021 and is still considered by many as one of the best coaches in the world.

The German has gone on to sign with Bavarian giant Bayern Munich through the 2024/25 season and recently told reporters he needed “quite a bit of time to distance himself from Chelsea” because leaving the club had hurt him.

Bayern Munich sacks manager Julian Nagelsmann, appoints Thomas Tuchel.

“Todd [Boehly] said he would be different to Roman [Abramovich],” former Liverpool player and current pundit Jamie Carragher wrote on Twitter.

“I feel for Graham Potter, but it was inevitable. You don’t change Tuchel for Potter. Ridiculous decision to start with.”.

With 10 games left in the league and a Champions League quarterfinal against Real Madrid on the horizon, Chelsea still has plenty to play for.

Assistant coach Bruno Saltor will take over on an interim basis, but Boehly and his team must now look for a long-term replacement capable – and willing – to bring order to Chelsea’s chaos.

Potter’s sacking is yet another sign of just how transient managers can be in the top-flight of English football, especially when results aren’t instantaneous.

There has now been a record 12 sackings in the Premier League so far this season, with Potter leaving his position the same day Leicester boss Brendan Rodgers was sacked from his.

The previous record was 10 manager changes in a single season, set in four other campaigns, most recently in 2017/18.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that NASA has released a $1 million Moon Base Challenge, inviting teams of students from high schools and colleges across the United States to help develop ideas for humanity's future on the Moon.
  • "We're looking for students ready to think creatively, work as a team, and take on real problems connected to NASA's future on the Moon," stated NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman.
  • NASA is working toward establishing a Moon Base near the lunar South Pole, where astronauts will be able to live, conduct research, and explore the surrounding region.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that NASA has released a $1 million Moon Base Challenge, inviting teams of students from high schools and colleges across the United States to help develop ideas for humanity's future on the Moon. The competition was announced during a MAX POWER event at Kennedy Space Center Visitor Complex in Florida. Presented as part of a Golden Age of Science, the initiative gives young innovators an opportunity to contribute designs and potential solutions for NASA's planned lunar base.

"We're looking for students ready to think creatively, work as a team, and take on real problems connected to NASA's future on the Moon," stated NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. "You do not have to wait until graduation to contribute. Curiosity, creativity, and the willingness to tackle hard problems without obvious answers are exactly the qualities we need as we build what comes next.".

NASA's Aims for a Permanent Moon Base.

NASA is working toward establishing a Moon Base near the lunar South Pole, where astronauts will be able to live, conduct research, and explore the surrounding region. Creating a lasting human presence on the Moon is also an crucial step toward future missions that will carry astronauts to Mars. Achieving these goals will require expertise and creative thinking from people across a wide range of industries and disciplines.

"As we build and design the foundations of Moon Base, we want to leverage all the ingenuity and innovation to think of every consideration our explorers might need to live and work there," mentioned Carlos García-Galán, manager, Moon Base Program. "Students bring exactly the bold ideas that we're looking for, and I'm looking forward to their fresh perspective. Ultimately, Moon Base is for them, people who will experience a world where humans are on the Moon to stay.".

Six Major Challenges of Living on the Moon.

In a recent development, the competition will unfold in multiple phases, with student teams developing solutions to six essential aspects of operating a lunar base. These include generating and storing power, constructing facilities, maintaining life support systems, enabling transportation across the lunar surface, establishing communications networks, and protecting astronauts.

Recent findings suggest that each category addresses practical obstacles that NASA must overcome to support long-term operations on the Moon. By working on these problems, students can explore newly introduced approaches to lunar technologies while developing technical and professional skills that could prepare them for careers in aerospace and related fields.

The challenge is designed around actual environmental conditions and mission requirements that would affect daily life and operations on the lunar surface. Participants will produce work similar to that used in the space industry, including evaluations of competing technical options, proposals outlining potential designs, and presentations for project stakeholders.

It has been revealed that students from technical, vocational, and other academic backgrounds are encouraged to participate. Previous specialized knowledge of engineering or related technical fields is not required, making the competition accessible to a broad range of young innovators.

Inspiring the Next Generation of Space Explorers.

Recent findings suggest that beyond generating ideas for the Moon Base, NASA hopes the competition will help develop the skills needed by the next generation of aerospace professionals. By exposing students to practical design challenges, the agency aims to encourage collaboration, creative problem-solving, and greater involvement in future space exploration.

Recent findings suggest that "Students are the next generation of explorers and innovators. Their unique perspectives are key to helping us envision a future away from Earth, and I'm excited to see the creativity and ingenuity spurred by this challenge," noted Elaine Ho, associate administrator for the Office of STEM Engagement at NASA Headquarters.

How to Enter NASA's $1 Million Moon Base Challenge.

Interested student teams must register through the NASA STEM Gateway. Registration remains open until January 25, 2027.

NASA's Office of STEM Engagement developed the competition in partnership with the agency's Moon Base Program. The Institute of Competition Sciences is responsible for administering the challenge under a contract with NASA's Center of Excellence for Collaborative Innovation, which operates within the Research and Technology Mission Directorate.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SpaceX launched a classified mission for the U.S. Space Force tonight (Nov. 20), sending a mystery payload to orbit from California's central coast.

It has been revealed that A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from Vandenberg Space Force Base tonight at 11:20 p.m. EST (8:20 p.m. local California time; 0420 GMT on Nov. 21), on a Space Force mission called USSF-317.

The Falcon 9's first stage came back to Earth about 8.5 minutes later, touching down in the Pacific Ocean atop the SpaceX drone ship "Of Course I Still Love You." It was the 11th launch and landing for this booster, which is designated B1100.

SpaceX ended its launch webcast just after that touchdown, so we didn't get to see the Falcon 9's upper stage power its way to orbit.

Industry observers note that USSF-317 is a classified mission, so we don't know what the upper stage is carrying or where exactly it's headed. However, some experts think that USSF-317 may be hauling a batch of SpaceX's Starshield satellites to low Earth orbit (LEO) for the Space Force's Space Based Sensing and Targeting portfolio, which helps the military keep tabs on potential targets around the world.

NROL-105 | USSF-385 | 8 Starlink missions.

USSF-317 was the 121st Falcon 9 launch of 2026 and the third mission that SpaceX has launched for the Space Force so far in November.

The vast majority of this year's Falcon 9 missions — about 70% of them — have been devoted to building out SpaceX's Starlink LEO internet constellation, which currently consists of more than 11,000 satellites.

The Falcon 9 has been putting up incredible numbers lately — it flew a whopping 165 times in 2025, for example — but the workhorse rocket is on its way out. SpaceX plans to retire both it and the Falcon Heavy in favor of its fully reusable Starship megarocket, which deployed 26 of SpaceX's next-gen Starlink V3 satellites on its most recent two test flights.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Manchester United's Premier League trip to Anfield was described by some as a free hit for new head coach Mauricio Pochettino.
  • The theory was expectations for United were so low as they travelled to Liverpool that a positive outcome would be a huge bonus, and anything else was expected.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Manchester United lost 4-0 at Liverpool in their opening match under Mauricio Pochettino.

Manchester United's Premier League trip to Anfield was described by some as a free hit for new head coach Mauricio Pochettino.

The theory was expectations for United were so low as they travelled to Liverpool that a positive outcome would be a huge bonus, and anything else was expected.

But Pochettino did not look like a man without pressure after 15 minutes of what turned into a 4-0 defeat.

According to recent reports, by that point, his side were already 2-0 behind and down to 10 men. Liverpool's fans were gleefully singing about the Argentine being "sacked in the morning", even though he was only a sixth of the way through his first game in charge.

A day later, United supporters began filtering through Manchester Airport on their way to Lisbon for a Champions League match that marks the next stop in what has turned into a desperate campaign.

The prevailing mood was one of resigned acceptance punctuated by dark humour around what a season in the Championship might look like, and whether Manchester City might be there with them.

United's England midfielder Kobbie Mainoo summed the situation up when he spoke to MUTV after the final whistle at Anfield.

"We're at the lowest we've ever been and no-one's coming to save us," mentioned the 21-year-old.

"There are no helping hands coming, so we've got to work together, lean on each other, keep working and hopefully it will come good.

"It's all about character now.".

Pochettino has signed a two-and-a-half-year contract.

United are giving little away about their looks for the January transfer window.

For now, it is being stressed, Pochettino's priority is to get the most from the players right now at his disposal.

However, there was sympathy with former boss Michael Carrick's belief he had been let down in the summer window and there was a plan to address that.

According to recent reports, that situation remains. A striker is thought to be Pochettino's priority given United's only recognised number nine, Benjamin Sesko, is out at least until January with a shin glitch that has bothered him since March.

United have a long-standing issue at left-back. First choice Luke Shaw missed his eighth successive game on Sunday and the only other orthodox left-back in senior ranks is England Under-20 international Harry Amass, who didn't even make the bench at Anfield.

However, Pochettino worked with Shaw at the start of his career at Southampton and feels the 31-year-old can be a positive influence on his group.

The reality though is United still have nine games to play before they can make any changes to their squad.

Among those fixtures are home games against Coventry, Nottingham Forest and Sunderland.

According to recent reports, newly promoted Coventry are four points ahead of United, who are second from bottom. Forest and Sunderland are in the two positions immediately above the Old Trafford club.

A trip to Crystal Palace - the one side below United, and the other Premier League club to replace their coach during the international break - looms on 13 December.

After Wednesday's encounter with Sporting, Pochettino's side have one Champions League game before the end of the year - against RB Leipzig on 8 December.

Any solutions to be found to the current mess over the next five weeks have to come from within. If they don't, light-hearted discussions about a first relegation since 1973-74 under Tommy Docherty start to get serious.

"They have got enough in that squad to get themselves out of the bottom three," Ashley Young - a Premier League winner with United - told Match of the Day.

It has been revealed that "They have not been showing that, but Pochettino has only just come in. He is going to want to get his team set up in a way that they are hard to beat. Right now, they do not look like they are hard to beat.

In a recent development, "It doesn't look like there is that togetherness. He has got to find a way to get that out of them. I am sure he will be able to do that when he has been longer in the job.".

Man Utd shouldn't worry about relegation right now - Young.

Pochettino shut down a question about United's terrible recent defensive record when he spoke to the media immediately after the game at Anfield.

"Tell me only about the circumstance today," he remarked. "I wasn't [here] in the past.".

That is true - and may also have been a useful diversion exercise in avoiding a dissection of a defensive unit he is still getting to know.

However, Pochettino knows United have kept one clean sheet all season - against Azerbaijani champions Sabah FK in September. He will also know United have now conceded 19 goals in their past six games.

Pochettino's big decision at Liverpool was to pick Matthijs de Ligt in the centre of a three-man defence ahead of Harry Maguire.

"He played in the Champions League you know, before the internationals," said the former Tottenham, PSG and Chelsea boss.

It was not clear when Pochettino meant.

In a recent development, in the 4-1 loss at Como on 21 October, De Ligt made his first appearance in 11 months following major back problems that eventually required surgery, largely because Leny Yoro was suspended and Lisandro Martinez was injured. He then played for two minutes against Roma on 3 November, when he was thrown on as then manager Carrick searched desperately for a winner.

Most goals can be broken down into a number of mistakes that compound to make an eventual negative outcome.

Team positioning has been mentioned as a reason De Ligt found himself exposed under a high ball at Anfield. However, his failure to deal with it presented Alexander Isak with a clear run at goal and prompted Yoro to make the tackle that led to his controversial dismissal, which Pochettino felt shaped the 82 minutes that followed.

It has been revealed that but United have been conceding bad goals all season. Numerous players have been culpable.

Sources indicate that there is a limit to what Pochettino can do in the time available. However, he wants to maximise what he can do.

Whereas Carrick tended to let his starting players have a day off after matches, the newly introduced regime has decided a warm-down session at Carrington is the better option.

And defensive organisation was surely one of the key points his coaching team had on their list of things to work on when the players began preparations to face Sporting on Wednesday.

Midfielder Andrey Santos has started three out of 10 Premier League games since the opening-day defeat at Hull.

With Â£70m summer arrival Carlos Baleba injured for the second time since the start of pre-season, Pochettino must find a way to protect United's goal, which might require additional support in midfield.

The strengths of Mainoo and Youri Tielemans are with the ball. Either with three in the middle of defence or a third man in midfield, a way needs to be found to stop opposition attacks running straight at the defence.

In his recent interview with Sky Sports, United chief executive Omar Berrada said the club needed to be "disciplined" in the transfer market and avoid spending huge sums on players who would not necessarily make the squad better.

But the fact former Chelsea midfielder Andrey Santos went five games between Premier League starts under Carrick from the opening-day defeat at Hull - and was only introduced for the final three minutes at Anfield - suggests there are doubts over the Brazilian, who cost Â£48m in the summer.

Underneath that is the knowledge United borrowed from their revolving credit facility around all their major summer purchases and did the same again earlier this month when Pochettino was hired at a cost of just over Â£7.5m.

In public accounts released last week, United confirmed there was another Â£160m available in credit - but also they owe Â£417m in outstanding transfer fees, Â£236m of which is due within 12 months.

Neither before nor after the transfer window opens do any simple solutions to United's predicament present themselves.

Last season, fellow 'substantial-six' club Tottenham did not save themselves until the final day of the season.

Confidence remains high at Old Trafford the situation will not be quite so dire for them, but it could be a very bumpy ride.

Bosses at soccer team Bayern Munich have publicly questioned whether young Germany international Jamal Musiala's contract is valid in view of a debilitating neurological condition.

The remarks have been criticized by media and from several other quarters, among them the global players' union FIFPRO, which accused the officials of neglecting their "duty of care" toward their players.

You can read details on what has been happening at the top football club in this DW article: Bayern Munich bosses under fire over Jamal Musiala comments.

Friedrich Christian "Mick" Flick, an art collector, investor and multimillionaire who belonged to one of Germany's richest business dynasties, has died aged 82 in Rosenheim in the southern state of Bavaria, his family has noted.

The family stated in a statement issued on Saturday that Flick left behind "the memory of a life shaped by significant acts of generosity as a donor and patron, particularly in contemporary art and in promoting tolerance.".

Flick was the grandson of Friedrich Flick, who made a huge fortune in the Nazi era with his coal and steel business, partly by using forced labor.

This past came back to haunt the grandson in 2003 when he pledged to loan his world-famous collection of modern art to Berlin, with the Central Council of Jews in Germany calling the Flick Collection a "Göring Collection" and saying the loan was intended to wash clean the "blood money" from the Nazi era.

The collection, which contains some 2,500 works by 150 artists, was exhibited in parts in the German capital from 2004 to 2021.

Flick later noted in an interview that the widespread outrage, while hurtful, had forced him to look more closely at his family's history.

Industry observers note that according to his family, Flick once noted: "I have no guilt for my forefathers' conduct, but I feel a responsibility, a very special responsibility. Every German bears this responsibility. As a Flick, I bear it twice.".

Among other things, he collaborated with the Prussian Cultural Heritage Foundation, which oversees Berlin's museums, to research his family's Nazi past.

He also set up a foundation in Potsdam, near Berlin, that aimed to combat xenophobia and racism and contributed €5 million ($5.4 million) to the foundation to compensate former forced laborers.

The family was also involved in a highly publicized party donations scandal in the 1980s that became known as the "Flick Affair.".

"Mick" Flick married Countess Maya von Schönburg (1958-2019), the older sister of well-known socialite, businesswoman, art collector and artist Gloria von Thurn und Taxis, in 1985. The couple had three children.

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is setting off on a five-day trip to Africa that will take him to Ivory Coast, Ghana and Kenya.

Steinmeier will be accompanied by a business delegation and is expected to focus on economic cooperation and the training of skilled workers during the trip.

On Monday, Steinmeier is to be received by Ivorian President Allassane Outtara in Abidjan, Ivory Coast's largest city and seat of government.

The next day, in the Ghanaian capital, Accra, he is set to open the German-African Business Summit, which, according to its website, "brings together senior business executives, policymakers, investors, and industry leaders from across Germany and Africa.".

On Wednesday, he will be received by Kenyan President William Ruto in Nairobi.

In Kenya, Steinmeier will also visit the Crescent Island Game Sanctuary on Thursday, the last day of his trip.

The Federal Institute for Hydrology (BfG) has said it expects water levels in large rivers in western Germany, including the Rhine, to return to average or above in the next few days amid sustained rainfall.

It said the water level at the key gauge in Kaub near Koblenz, located at an vital bottleneck on the Middle Rhine, could reach some 3.3 meters (10.8 feet), more than 3 meters higher than the last recorded low-water readings.

The BfG noted it also expected rising water levels in the Weser and Danube rivers, with smaller increases in the Elbe and Oder.

The rising water level in the Rhine, an important shipping route, means that conditions for water-borne cargo transport have improved, according to Germany's inland navigation association BDB.

"The more abundant rainfall in the past days has caused the water level in the Rhine to rise considerably, and they will keep rising a great deal in the next few days as well, meaning that each ship has much more transport capacity again," said Fabian Spiess, the deputy manager at BDB.

In the middle of the year, many ships were forced to drastically reduce the loads they carried, leading to economic losses that will not be recuperated any time soon, according to Spiess.

He cited the year 2018, in which shipping on the Rhine was also hindered by extremely low water levels, saying that the months of improved conditions at the end of that year had not been enough to make good the economic damage incurred.

The conservation NGO also stated that the current rain provided temporary relief to the environment but could not compensate for the negative consequences of the long dry period.

It noted species of animals, such as amphibians and water insects, that lived in small bodies of water and moist habitats had been particularly impacted.

Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig indicates that she intends to tighten the law on murders committed with "gender-specific" motives, with a particular focus on femicides perpetrated by men who are unable to accept a separation or the desire of a woman to live a self-determined life.

"A man kills, or attempts to kill, his partner or ex-partner almost every day in Germany," Hubig told the Sunday edition of the mass-circulation Bild newspaper.

"Any man killing a woman because she wants to leave him must be punished as a murderer," she said, noting that in some cases, courts cite a man's deep sadness or fear of losing a partner to someone else as extenuating circumstances. This can lead to a lesser conviction of manslaughter.

She mentioned that in future, courts should look more closely at such motives to determine whether they were based on sentiments of patriarchal possessiveness.

However, Hubig, who belongs to the center-left Social Democrats (SPD), mentioned she was opposed to making femicide a separate category of crime, as some women's rights organizations have demanded.

She mentioned that, in her opinion, doing so would have "no advantages over what we are intending — and much bigger disadvantages.".

The proposals are presently being debated within the coalition government and are expected to be presented to the states and associations for consideration before the end of the year.

They will then have to go before the Cabinet before being put before the parliament.

The powerful IG Metall union noted on Sunday it would call another 24-hour strike on Monday as a pay dispute continues.

Altogether, some 23,000 workers at 19 companies in northern Germany have been called upon to participate, including employees at automaker Mercedes-Benz, shipbuilding manufacturer Meyer Werft and wind ​energy company Siemens Gamesa.

The union said that a strike on Friday saw some 12,300 workers walk out at 17 facilities.

It states that the strikes are meant to increase the pressure on employers to yield to its demands, which include a 5% ‌wage increase.

So far, employers have ⁠offered a one-off payment next year and a 1.3% wage increase from July 2028.

The DW newsroom states "Willkommen!" once more to all its readers as we resume our reporting on all things German.

Some good news is on the agenda: The Rhine River, which we can see from the window of our Bonn office, has recovered after a long period with little rainfall, meaning that the barges plying the waterway can load up properly again.

In other stories, the German president, Frank-Walter Steinmeier, is setting off on a trip to Africa, during which he is set to visit three countries with a businesss delegation in tow.

And Germany's powerful IG Metall union has said it is launching another 24-hour strike on Monday amid an escalating pay dispute.

Read on to find out more about what is happening in Germany on Sunday, November 22.

We're pausing our Germany news blog for now. Come back for more on Sunday!

A fresh goal celebration was devised by Borussia Dortmund midfielder Felix Nmecha after his previous one caused controversy due to its religious aspect.

Sources indicate that after scoring the goal that secured Dortmund's 1-0 victory over Borussia Mönchengladbach (see entry below), Nmecha knelt on one knee and crossed his arms in front of his chest. He then spread his arms, appearing to pray with his eyes closed.

Nmecha told broadcaster Sky that he intends to continue expressing his faith during goal celebrations, adding that he had once again given glory to Jesus.

In a recent development, however, he did not perform the controversial part of his usual goal celebration. In it, he removes an imaginary crown from his head and places it on the pitch in front of him while kneeling.

This celebration has been heavily criticized, even by Dortmund's fan department.

Nmecha explained that the celebrations is about "putting down my 'crown' in front of the soon-to-come king and point out to Jesus, my hope and my strength.".

The gesture is used by Ballers in God, a network of Christian football players that has been criticized for the homophobic and queerphobic statements made by its members.

Dortmund president Hans-Joachim Watzke said he asked the player not to do the celebration again.

Borussia Dortmund midfielder Felix Nmecha led his team to the top of the German Bundesliga table with a 1-0 victory over last-place Borussia Mönchengladbach.

Meanwhile, Bayern Munich was held to a 1-1 draw at home by Cologne on Friday, and striker Harry Kane suffered a serious ankle injury. The Ballon d'Or winner is set to miss several months after undergoing ankle surgery earlier on Saturday.

Now, Dortmund has 24 points after 10 games, putting them two points ahead of Bayern and third-place Freiburg, who defeated Elversberg 1-0.

Sources indicate that fourth-place RB Leipzig had five different players score in a 5-1 victory over Union Berlin, bringing them to 21 points. Bayer Leverkusen scored four unanswered goals against Paderborn to stay in fifth place.

Germany is seeking to redress years of underinvestment by pouring billions into the modernization of public infrastructure and digital networks, and the transition to renewable energy sources.

But will the plan bring real change amid the labor shortages, burdensome bureaucracy and low productivity currently besetting Europe's largest economy?

DW takes a look at what is one of Germany's biggest public investment drives in decades in this video:.

Bundesliga powerhouse Bayern Munich concluded the 2025-26 financial year with record figures.

According to the financial report released Saturday at the club's annual general meeting, the club's total turnover was €988.2 million ($1.08 billion) — that is around €10 million more than the previous year.

Operating profit (EBITDA) increased from €187.8 million to €190.8 million. Pre-tax profit was €35.3 million, and net profit for the year was €22.8 million.

It has been revealed that bayern had a particularly strong year in terms of sponsorships. Turnover increased by nearly €30 million, reaching €268.4 million. The club also set a record in merchandise sales, earning €152.8 million.

Members hold a 70% stake in the club, which is well above the simple majority required by German rules.

Bayern won the league and cup double in the 2025-26 season, losing only three of 53 games across all competitions. In Europe, the club made it to the Champions League semifinals.

England captain Kane, who finished the 2025–26 season with over 70 goals for club and country, was awarded the Ballon d'Or for his efforts.

Tech Report: European-Japanese BepiColombo mission becomes 2nd ever to arrive in orbit around Mercury

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (892 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, update for 2:50 p.m.
  • For just the second time ever, Mercury has received a robotic visitor from Earth.
  • The BepiColombo mission — a joint effort of the European Space Agency (ESA) and the Japanese Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) — arrived in orbit around Mercury on Saturday (Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, update for 2:50 p.m. ET on Nov. 23: On Sunday afternoon (Nov. 22), the BepiColombo team unveiled that, while the spacecraft did successfully arrive in orbit around Mercury on Saturday (Nov. 21), the engine burn that got it there was cut short due to a software glitch. On Monday (Nov. 23), we got another update: BepiColombo "is safe and in a stable orbit around Mercury" and is on track for the next massive milestone: The separation of its two orbiters on Dec. 9.

For just the second time ever, Mercury has received a robotic visitor from Earth.

The BepiColombo mission — a joint effort of the European Space Agency (ESA) and the Japanese Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) — arrived in orbit around Mercury on Saturday (Nov. 21), more than eight years after leaving its home planet.

Before BepiColombo, just one spacecraft had ever circled the solar system's innermost planet: NASA's MESSENGER, which did so from March 2011 to April 2015.

BepiColombo consists of two main spacecraft: ESA's Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and JAXA's Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (MMO), also known as Mio.

The duo rolled out — along with a power and propulsion element called the Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) — aboard an Ariane 5 rocket from French Guiana in October 2018, beginning a long and looping trip through the inner solar system.

It has been revealed that mercury is a difficult planet to reach because it's so close to the sun. Spacecraft approaching the planet are accelerated to high velocities by the immense gravitational pull of our star and must therefore shed a great deal of kinetic energy to be captured by Mercury's much weaker tug.

So the BepiColombo team designed a trajectory that featured one flyby of Earth, two of Venus and six of Mercury over the course of about seven years. That flight time was increased by a year, however, after the mission suffered an issue with its solar panels, which reduced the power available for the MTM's electric thrusters.

Recent findings suggest that saturday's orbital insertion came after a 37-minute-long engine burn, which began at 1:24 p.m. EST (1824 GMT). There was a bit drama involved, however, as confirmation of the maneuver's success didn't come for several hours afterward.

"We've heard back from Bepi — the spacecraft is now in contact with the ground and the teams at ESOC [the European Space Operations Centre] are busy assessing the telemetry. Flight Dynamics already has confirmed it achieved orbital capture around Mercury! Early next week we'll share the next update with the upcoming steps," the mission team noted via X on Saturday evening.

We've heard back from Bepi - the spacecraft is now in contact with the ground and the teams at ESOC are busy assessing the telemetry. Flight Dynamics already has confirmed it achieved orbital capture around Mercury! Early next week we'll share the next update with the upcoming steps.November 22, 2026.

Orbital insertion is the latest milestone in BepiColombo's Mercury arrival phase, which is expected to take about six months in total.

Arrival began on Sept. 3, when the MTM released MPO and Mio. The two orbiters remain connected today; they won't separate until Dec. 9 or thereabouts.

Shortly thereafter, Mio will settle into its final orbit, a highly elliptical path that will take it over Mercury's poles. MPO is also destined for a polar orbit, though a much less elliptical one than Mio's; the ESA probe will conduct a series of engine burns before finally getting there on March 10, 2027.

Sources indicate that bepiColombo — which is named after the late Italian scientist and mathematician Giuseppe "Bepi" Colombo — won't start doing science work until April 6, 2027. The two probes will gather complementary data from their different vantage points, shedding a great deal of light on a mysterious world.

"The mission will study all aspects of Mercury, from the structure and dynamics of its magnetosphere and how it interacts with the solar wind, to its internal structure with its large iron core, and the origin of the planet’s magnetic field," ESA officials wrote in a BepiColombo mission description.

"The data will enable scientists to understand more about the origin and evolution of a planet located close to its parent star, and a better understanding of the overall evolution of our solar system," they added.

In a recent development, editor's note: This story was updated at 11:15 a.m. ET on Nov. 22 with news off successful orbital arrival.

ESA’s Hera spacecraft is flying rectangles around NASA’s asteroid crash site

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1023 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The European Space Agency's Hera spacecraft has reached its destination, arriving near two asteroids that could help scientists learn how to protect Earth from dangerous space rocks.
  • This initial stage, known as the "early characterization phase," is designed to give researchers a broad understanding of the two asteroids and their surroundings.
  • "Our aim right now is to gather the major-picture findings of relevance to supporting the mission's planetary defense goals," explains mission scientist Michael Kueppers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The European Space Agency's Hera spacecraft has reached its destination, arriving near two asteroids that could help scientists learn how to protect Earth from dangerous space rocks. The spacecraft, which is roughly the size of a small car, is now traveling about 25 to 30 kilometers from the Didymos asteroid system as it begins its first scientific observations.

This initial stage, known as the "early characterization phase," is designed to give researchers a broad understanding of the two asteroids and their surroundings. Of particular interest is Dimorphos, the smaller asteroid that NASA deliberately struck with its DART spacecraft in 2022 to test whether a collision could change an asteroid's path.

"Our aim right now is to gather the major-picture findings of relevance to supporting the mission's planetary defense goals," explains mission scientist Michael Kueppers.

"During this phase, our images will reveal for the first time what a small asteroid looks like globally, having experienced a hypervelocity impact in the context of the first asteroid deflection test, when NASA's DART spacecraft impacted it to change its orbit in 2022.".

"Previous predictions by our impact models suggested many different ways the asteroid body might react, but Hera will reveal which forecast was the correct one - if any!".

Why Hera Is Flying in Rectangles Around Two Asteroids.

Navigating around asteroids presents challenges that are very different from those encountered by spacecraft exploring planets. The main asteroid, Didymos, measures approximately 780 meters across and has gravitational pull about 40,000 times weaker than Earth's. Its smaller companion, Dimorphos, is just 151 meters wide and has gravity roughly 200,000 times weaker than Earth's.

Sources indicate that with gravity this weak, maintaining a conventional circular orbit is not practical. Hera instead travels around the shared center of gravity of the two asteroids, moving at a remarkably slow speed of approximately 12 centimeters per second. That is comparable to the pace of an insect crawling rapidly across the ground.

Sources indicate that rather than following a smooth circular path, Hera moves along nearly straight trajectories. At alternating intervals of three and four days, the spacecraft fires its thrusters while moving away from the asteroids, changing direction by 90 degrees. These carefully timed maneuvers create a series of unusual "rectangular orbits" that keep Hera approximately 25 to 30 kilometers from the asteroid pair.

The unusual navigation strategy builds on experience gained during ESA's Rosetta comet mission. It also provides an notable safety advantage. If a planned thruster firing fails, Hera will naturally drift farther from the asteroids instead of moving toward a potentially dangerous collision. Because the spacecraft travels so slowly, each course correction requires very little propellant.

Hera Prepares for a Closer Look at the Asteroids.

Next month, Hera is expected to begin its "detailed characterization phase," bringing it significantly closer to Didymos and Dimorphos. During this stage, the spacecraft will switch from rectangular flight paths to more complex hyperbolic trajectories shaped like bowties, beginning at distances of approximately 20 kilometers.

Recent findings suggest that the mission is directed from ESA's ESOC mission control center in Darmstadt, Germany. Despite Hera being approximately 196.5 million kilometers from Earth, controllers maintain contact with the spacecraft for about eight hours each day.

Communication is handled through four enormous Deep Space Antennas, each measuring 35 meters in diameter, at facilities in Argentina, Spain, and Australia.

According to recent reports, the mission control team also works closely with ESA's Flight Dynamics team. Using data transmitted by Hera, these specialists calculate its exact location relative to the two asteroids and develop the commands needed to guide it safely from one planned position to another.

Investigating NASA's Historic Asteroid Collision.

Hera's observations will help answer some of the biggest questions left unanswered by NASA's first asteroid deflection experiment.

On September 26, 2022, NASA's DART spacecraft deliberately collided with Dimorphos. The 580-kilogram spacecraft struck the asteroid at approximately 6.1 kilometers per second, producing a massive cloud of debris that spread across 10,000 kilometers of space.

It has been revealed that the impact successfully changed Dimorphos' motion, shortening the time it takes to orbit Didymos by about 33 minutes. This was a major achievement for planetary defense, demonstrating that deliberately crashing a spacecraft into an asteroid could alter its trajectory.

According to recent reports, however, the experiment also raised important questions. Scientists still do not know exactly how the impact changed Dimorphos itself. Did the collision excavate a large crater, or did it significantly reshape the entire asteroid?

Researchers also need more precise information about Dimorphos' composition, internal structure, and mass. Understanding these properties could explain why the impact produced a much larger orbital change than computer simulations had predicted.

Recent findings suggest that these details are essential for developing the collision method, known as kinetic impact, into a dependable planetary defense strategy. If scientists can determine how different types of asteroids respond to being struck, they will be better equipped to predict the results of future attempts to redirect potentially hazardous objects.

A Close-Up Investigation of the Asteroid Crash Site.

Over the coming months, Hera will conduct a detailed investigation of Dimorphos, effectively examining the scene of NASA's historic collision.

The spacecraft will use several scientific instruments to study the asteroid and will release two small CubeSats, each about the size of a shoebox. These miniature spacecraft will travel even closer to the asteroid to collect additional measurements, with the mission eventually advancing to landing operations.

In a recent development, together, the observations should provide scientists with a much clearer understanding of how Dimorphos responded to DART's impact and why the experiment worked so effectively. That knowledge could prove crucial if Earth ever faces a dangerous asteroid on a collision course.

#162267. Latest Update: A Power Provider for Meta Urged Regulators to Exempt Data Center Plants From Acid Rain Rules

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1497 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: A Power Provider for Meta Urged Regulators to Exempt Data Center Plants From Acid Rain Rules

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1497 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Williams, a provider of gas power to several Meta data centers, met with Environmental Protection Agency leaders in the period leading up to the agency’s recommendation to waive acid rain regulations for data-center power plants, documents obtained by WIRED show.
  • The oil and gas infrastructure company’s private discussions with the agency come as the Trump administration loosens a number of environmental requirements for data centers and the natural gas plants being built to power them.
  • It has been revealed that “The administration is trying to relax, if not suspend for all intents and purposes, a range of regulatory requirements for these data centers,” says Joseph Goffman, the former assistant administrator at the EPA’s Office of Air and Radiation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Williams, a provider of gas power to several Meta data centers, met with Environmental Protection Agency leaders in the period leading up to the agency’s recommendation to waive acid rain regulations for data-center power plants, documents obtained by WIRED show.

The oil and gas infrastructure company’s private discussions with the agency come as the Trump administration loosens a number of environmental requirements for data centers and the natural gas plants being built to power them.

It has been revealed that “The administration is trying to relax, if not suspend for all intents and purposes, a range of regulatory requirements for these data centers,” says Joseph Goffman, the former assistant administrator at the EPA’s Office of Air and Radiation. “What this administration is trying to do, either explicitly or de facto, is take layers [of regulatory protections] away.”.

In response to a list of questions from WIRED, Williams spokesperson Alex Schott mentioned in an emailed statement that the manufacturer “is committed to developing energy solutions to enhance America’s position in the global competition for AI, while prioritizing environmental protection—including addressing legislation and regulations to modernize construction and implementation timelines.” Meta declined to comment.

In July, the EPA confirmed upcoming federal guidance for states around participation in the Acid Rain Program, following inquiries from “companies and States.” The decades-old program was designed to reduce harmful emissions of chemicals that cause acid rain. Power plants that fall under the program need to submit a permit application two years before a facility comes online, and then regularly monitor emissions to ensure compliance.

That month, the EPA said that it recommends that “islanded” power plants—which are increasingly being adopted by data centers across the country—be exempt from the program. Because the program was designed for facilities that sell electricity to the grid, the EPA said, power plants that exclusively power data centers wouldn’t need to comply.

Documents obtained by WIRED from the EPA show that Williams was one of three private companies that asked regulators for guidance on the program.

In a February letter sent to the Utah Department of Environmental Quality and obtained by WIRED, Williams director of permitting Steve Hall wrote that the “current regulatory uncertainty” around power plants being built solely to power data centers has created “obstacles … for data center development in the United States.” The EPA confirmed to WIRED that Williams sent the agency this letter.

Hall wrote that the manufacturer believed its power plants “are not subject to the Acid Rain Permit program requirements, as this program was never intended to apply to sources that do not sell power to the public grid.” Getting federal guidance, he wrote, would “accelerate deployment of critical infrastructure” and “support national goals for digital infrastructure and energy reliability in the global AI race.”.

Industry observers note that the EPA stated in its July announcement that the upcoming guidance was in keeping with orders from the White House to encourage data center developers to build their own power, in order to avoid increasing utility rates for consumers. However, data center developers are also increasingly turning to private power because it’s often quicker to build their own infrastructure than wait for a grid connection. These private power plants often create more emissions than many of their on-grid counterparts.

Sources indicate that williams, one of the top oil and gas infrastructure companies in the country, has emerged in recent years as a power provider for data centers. As of November, Williams had at least six data-center power plant projects in states across the country. Meta is the client for at least four of those projects: four in Ohio, and one in Utah.

According to recent reports, calendar invites provided by EPA show that Hall and other executives were invited to at least two meetings with EPA officials, including at least one with Aaron Szabo, then the chief of the agency’s Air office, earlier this year. In an external meeting request form filed with the agency in April, Williams indicated that its request to discuss projects in Ohio and Utah—sites where it is building power plants for Meta—was “urgent.”.

The EPA confirmed to WIRED that Williams “requested regulatory guidance for both projects” in Ohio and Utah, and that the meetings “broadly discussed air regulations.”.

“EPA program offices regularly meet with stakeholders in their areas of jurisdiction,” the agency added.

Williams’ materials submitted to regulators did not specifically reference its relationship with Meta. But in its official letter on the rule recommendations, the EPA used an example provided by an unnamed organization that is building a planned 500-megawatt power plant of simple-cycle natural gas engines “to exclusively power an adjacent, third-party-owned data center.” Williams’ project in Utah and two of its projects in Ohio to power Meta data centers are around 500 megawatts each.

In a recent development, williams first publicly proposed the exemption to the Acid Rain Program in September 2025 in testimony to the House of Representatives from Mark Gebbia, then the organization’s vice president of environmental, permitting, and regulatory affairs. In the testimony, Gebbia made several suggestions as to how EPA should change or clarify the implementation of the Clean Air Act, including exempting behind-the-meter data centers from Acid Rain Program requirements. He noted that the long timelines for the permits are “not feasible given the urgent need to install and operate gas-fired generation for AI data centers.”.

According to recent reports, the Acid Rain Program has long been considered a regulatory success that’s ensured coal plants reduce emissions of sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, pollutants that help create acid rain. The law created a cap-and-trade program for power plants, allowing them to buy and sell credits for emissions to keep national levels of the pollutants low.

Natural gas plants emit lower levels of these pollutants than traditional coal-fired power plants. The permit application for Williams’ facility to power Meta’s data center in Utah, for example, shows that it could emit a maximum of around 100 tons of nitrogen oxide and 11 tons of sulfur dioxide each year. A 500-megawatt coal plant, meanwhile, can emit thousands of tons per year of each of those pollutants.

According to recent reports, other local and national restrictions may limit how much of these pollutants come from natural gas plants. But Acid Rain Program regulations also created crucial reporting requirements that are now in jeopardy for data-center power plants. In the early 1990s, Congress passed an amendment to the Clean Air Act mandating that power facilities monitor and report various emissions in order to establish the program. The reporting requirement covers sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, as well as carbon dioxide, the main driver of climate change.

The Obama administration later set up a program that would separate CO2 reporting requirements, though the Trump administration has made moves to repeal that program.

Now, exempting data-center power plants from complying with the acid rain regulations may jeopardize how much information regulators eventually get about data center emissions—including CO2 emissions, Goffman states.

“If the Trump administration was not deranged, and the greenhouse gas reporting program was operating, I think the EPA would be either interpreting that program’s existing requirements to cover these gas plants, or they would be promulgating new regulations to ensure these new gas plants were reporting their greenhouse gas emissions,” he says.

Both Goffman and Carrie Jenks, who directs the Environmental and Energy Law Program at Harvard Law School, agree that the EPA’s guidance on the Acid Rain Program for data centers seems to stick to the letter of the law. The program, they say, was explicitly intended to apply only to power plants that sold power to the grid. (Some environmental groups disagree with Goffman and Jenks: Earthjustice and the NRDC sent a letter to the EPA in September challenging the agency’s interpretation of the law in its July recommendation.).

According to recent reports, when the program was created in 1990, though, wealthy tech companies weren’t rushing to build hundreds of megawatts of private fossil-fuel power that may not ever be connected to the grid. “No one expected it to be economical to develop a bunch of power plants that wouldn’t sell the product they were creating. No one envisioned this,” Jenks notes. The program “was never designed to address behind-the-meter generation,” she says.

Some estimates show that there’s more than 110 gigawatts of planned behind-the-meter gas projects in the US, with some facilities—like Amazon’s 7-gigawatt facility in Texas, and SoftBank’s 9.2-gigawatt project in Ohio—on track to be some of the largest natural gas plants in the world. Even if those facilities don’t technically qualify for the Acid Rain Program because they’re not on the grid, lawmakers could move to change requirements to make sure that these massive facilities are covered by the program.

Sources indicate that “Congress should have the ability and the authority to say, we have this situation, it wasn’t anticipated, here is the law,” Jenks states. “If the world were working, that’s what should happen.”.
